title: Quiz: the variational autoencoder
text:
Short questions on clouds, the prior and the VAE loss. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. The encoder gives each image a cloud \mathcal N(\mu, \sigma^2); the decoder is trained on draws z = \mu + \sigma\varepsilon; the loss is reconstruction +\ \beta\cdot\mathrm{KL}, with \mathrm{KL} = \tfrac12(\mu^2 + s^2 - 1 - \ln s^2) per dimension.

Q1. In a plain autoencoder each image becomes one point; in a VAE a small cloud. Give two things the cloud buys you.






Hint





What must the decoder do with random points from the cloud? What does the prior do to all the clouds?









Answer






The decoder is trained on random points around each image, and all clouds are pulled towards one standard cloud, so they overlap: the latent space has few gaps, and points near and between images decode to sensible images. That is what makes generating possible. (2) The spread says how sure the encoder is about where the image belongs.





Q2. Compute the KL to the prior of the clouds \mathcal N(0, 1), \mathcal N(1, 1) and \mathcal N(0, 0.5^2).






Hint





\tfrac12(\mu^2 + s^2 - 1 - \ln s^2), and \ln 0.25 = -1.386.









Answer





0; \tfrac12(1 + 1 - 1 - 0) = 0.5; \tfrac12(0 + 0.25 - 1 + 1.386) = 0.318.




Q3. What would a VAE learn if the loss had only the KL term? And with only the reconstruction term?






Hint





Which cloud makes the KL zero? What is the cheapest way to rebuild perfectly?









Answer





Only KL: every image gets the prior as its cloud, so z carries no information and the decoder outputs the same (average) image for everything. Only reconstruction: the clouds shrink to points and can sit anywhere, far apart: a plain autoencoder, with gaps.




Q4. The encoder gives \mu = 0.4, \sigma = 0.2. With \varepsilon = 1.5, what is z? Why is z written this way instead of being drawn directly from \mathcal N(0.4, 0.2^2)?






Hint





z = \mu + \sigma\varepsilon.









Answer





z = 0.4 + 0.2 \cdot 1.5 = 0.7. Written as a formula in \mu and \sigma, z changes smoothly when the encoder changes \mu or \sigma, so the training can compute how the loss changes with the encoder’s weights (the gradient). A direct draw would hide that dependence.




Q5. You increase \beta from 1 to 5. What happens to the clouds, and to the reconstructed images?






Hint





Which of the two forces gets stronger?









Answer





The pull towards the prior gets stronger: clouds move towards 0 and get wider, so neighbouring images overlap more and the latent space is tidier. The decoder must serve wider clouds with one image each, so reconstructions get blurrier and less specific.




Q6. (math) True or false: a VAE trained with \beta = 1 maximises a lower bound on the log-probability of the training images.






Hint





ELBO stands for evidence lower bound.









Answer





True. The loss with \beta = 1 is minus the ELBO, and the ELBO is at most \ln p(x); the gap is the KL between the encoder’s cloud and the true posterior of z given the image.

title: Exercise: the variational autoencoder
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

explain what the encoder’s cloud and the prior do, and why the decoder is fed random draws,
draw a point of a cloud with the reparameterisation z = \mu + \sigma\varepsilon,
compute the KL divergence of a Gaussian cloud to the prior, and the two terms of the VAE loss for a small example,
predict how the best cloud moves when the image or \beta changes.

The questions under By hand and Explore are for everyone. The Math questions (derive, prove) are for students who want the full treatment.

title: Exercise: the variational autoencoder
text:
Background







Word
Meaning




Encoder cloud
q(z\mid x) = \mathcal N(\mu, s^2): where in latent space image x belongs, and how sure


Prior
the standard cloud \mathcal N(0, 1) (in k dimensions \mathcal N(0, I))


Reparameterisation
z = \mu + s\,\varepsilon with \varepsilon \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)


KL to the prior
\tfrac12(\mu^2 + s^2 - 1 - \ln s^2) per latent dimension; dimensions add


VAE loss
reconstruction +\ \beta\cdot\mathrm{KL}; \beta = 1 is the standard VAE



The one-dimensional VAE of the lecture and the demo: one grey value x, decoder \hat x = wz with w = 1 and pixel noise \sigma_x = 0.5. Its reconstruction term is
R(\mu, s) = \frac{(x - w\mu)^2 + w^2 s^2}{2\sigma_x^2},
the average squared error over the cloud, divided by 2\sigma_x^2.

title: Exercise: the variational autoencoder
text:
By hand

Part A — clouds and draws
B1. The encoder gives \mu = 1, s = 0.5. Using the reparameterisation, compute z for \varepsilon = -1, 0 and 0.5. Where do 95% of all draws fall?
B2. Two digits, a 4 and a 9, have cloud centres 0.3 apart and spreads 0.06. Would you expect their clouds to overlap (within ±2 sd)? What does the decoder produce halfway between them?
B3. Explain in two sentences what goes wrong if the decoder is always given the centre \mu instead of a random draw.


Part B — the KL penalty
B4. Compute the KL to the prior for the clouds (\mu, s) = (0.5, 1), (0, 2) and (2, 0.1). (\ln 4 = 1.386, \ln 0.01 = -4.605.) Rank them, and say what each one is “punished” for.
B5. In 2D, a cloud has centre (1, 0) and spreads (0.5, 1). What is its KL to \mathcal N(0, I)?


Part C — the two forces, with numbers
Use x = 1.5, w = 1, \sigma_x = 0.5, \beta = 1.
B6. Compute R, KL and the total loss for the cloud \mu = 1, s = 0.5. Compare with the table in the lecture: is it better or worse than the prior, the “too confident” cloud and the best cloud?
B7. Without computing: if the image were x = 0 instead, where would the best cloud’s centre be? And for x = 3?
B8. Without computing: with \beta = 5, does the best \mu move towards 0 or towards x? Does s get larger or smaller?






Solutions





B1. z = 1 + 0.5\varepsilon: 0.5, 1, 1.25. 95% of draws fall within \mu \pm 2s, i.e. between 0 and 2.
B2. No: within ±2 sd each cloud reaches 0.12 from its centre, so the two clouds together cover 0.24 of the 0.3 between them. But the gap is small, and the KL penalty pulls all clouds together, so the decoder is trained on points near both and the halfway point decodes to a blend: an image that looks partly like a 4 and partly like a 9.
B3. Then each image is only ever decoded at one point, and nothing trains the decoder at points around it: we are back to a plain autoencoder with gaps. The random draw forces a whole neighbourhood of each image to decode to that image.
B4. (0.5, 1): \tfrac12(0.25 + 1 - 1 - 0) = 0.125, punished only for its shifted centre. (0, 2): \tfrac12(0 + 4 - 1 - 1.386) = 0.807, punished for being too wide. (2, 0.1): \tfrac12(4 + 0.01 - 1 + 4.605) = 3.808, punished both for its far centre and for being very narrow (very sure). Order: 0.125 < 0.807 < 3.808.
B5. The dimensions add: first dimension \tfrac12(1 + 0.25 - 1 - \ln 0.25) = \tfrac12(0.25 + 1.386) = 0.818, second \tfrac12(0 + 1 - 1 - 0) = 0. Total 0.818.
B6. R = \big((1.5 - 1)^2 + 0.25\big)/(2 \cdot 0.25) = 0.5/0.5 = 1.000. KL = 0.818 (B5, first dimension). Total 1.818: much better than the prior (6.500) and the too-confident cloud (3.627), a little worse than the best cloud (1.705).
B7. For x = 0 both forces agree: the best centre is \mu = 0 (with s below 1, because the image still pins z down). For x = 3 the centre moves out, but stays short of 3, pulled back towards the prior (B10: \mu = 2.4).
B8. Towards 0, and s gets larger: the prior’s pull is five times stronger, so the cloud moves towards \mathcal N(0, 1) in both centre and width.





Math questions
B9. (math) Derive the KL formula from \mathrm{KL}(q\|p) = \mathbb E_q[\ln q(z) - \ln p(z)] for q = \mathcal N(\mu, s^2), p = \mathcal N(0, 1). Show that it is \ge 0 with equality only at \mu = 0, s = 1.
B10. (math) Minimise R(\mu, s) + \beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\mu, s) over \mu and s^2. Give the best cloud for \beta = 1 and \beta = 5, and check B7–B8.
B11. (math) Show \ln p(x) - \text{ELBO} = \mathrm{KL}\big(q(z)\,\|\,p(z\mid x)\big), using p(x\mid z)\,p(z) = p(z\mid x)\,p(x).






Solutions (math)





B9. (math) \ln q(z) = -\tfrac12\ln(2\pi s^2) - (z - \mu)^2/(2s^2), \ln p(z) = -\tfrac12\ln 2\pi - z^2/2. Under q: \mathbb E[(z - \mu)^2] = s^2, \mathbb E[z^2] = \mu^2 + s^2. So \mathrm{KL} = -\tfrac12\ln s^2 - \tfrac12 + \tfrac12(\mu^2 + s^2) = \tfrac12(\mu^2 + s^2 - 1 - \ln s^2). With t = s^2, f(t) = t - 1 - \ln t has f'(t) = 1 - 1/t, a minimum at t = 1 with f(1) = 0; so f \ge 0, and \mu^2 \ge 0; equality needs \mu = 0 and s = 1.
B10. (math) \partial/\partial\mu: -w(x - w\mu)/\sigma_x^2 + \beta\mu = 0 \Rightarrow \mu^* = wx/(w^2 + \beta\sigma_x^2). \partial/\partial s^2: w^2/(2\sigma_x^2) + \tfrac\beta2(1 - 1/s^2) = 0 \Rightarrow s^{*2} = \beta\sigma_x^2/(\beta\sigma_x^2 + w^2). With w = 1, \sigma_x^2 = 0.25, x = 1.5: \beta = 1: \mu^* = 1.5/1.25 = 1.2, s^{*2} = 0.25/1.25 = 0.2 (s^* = 0.447); \beta = 5: \mu^* = 1.5/2.25 = 0.667, s^{*2} = 1.25/2.25 = 0.556 (s^* = 0.745). B7: x = 0 gives \mu^* = 0; x = 3 gives \mu^* = 2.4, s^* unchanged (0.447): the spread does not depend on x in this model. B8: \mu^* falls from 1.2 to 0.667 and s^* rises from 0.447 to 0.745.
B11. (math) \text{ELBO} = \mathbb E_q[\ln p(x\mid z) + \ln p(z) - \ln q(z)] = \mathbb E_q[\ln p(z\mid x) + \ln p(x) - \ln q(z)] = \ln p(x) - \mathbb E_q[\ln q(z) - \ln p(z\mid x)] = \ln p(x) - \mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p(z\mid x)).

title: Exercise: the variational autoencoder
text:
Explore
The demo is the one-dimensional VAE above for one image value x. Top: the prior (dashed) and the encoder’s cloud q (orange) with 20 draws z = \mu + s\varepsilon (fixed \varepsilon). Middle: the draws decoded, wz (blue), and the image value x (red triangles). Bottom: the reconstruction term, \beta\timesKL and the total, with the best possible total in green. The readout also gives the reconstruction term estimated from the 20 draws, as training would compute it.



E1. At the start, q is the prior. Read the three bars. Drag \mu to 1.5 with s = 1: which term changes, and by how much? Then shrink s: what happens to the blue dots and to each term?
E2. Press best cloud for this x and β. Read \mu, s and the three numbers. Compare with B6 and the lecture’s table.
E3. Preset too confident. Which term is large? Why does the training not simply make every cloud a point at the right place?
E4. Preset best (β = 5). How do \mu and s change compared with \beta = 1? Which term is now the larger one? Then set \beta to 0 and press best cloud: what happens, and why is this a problem for generating images?
E5. Back at the prior (preset ignore the image), compare the exact reconstruction term with the estimate from the 20 draws. Then press best cloud and compare again. Why do they differ, and why can training still work with such estimates?






Solutions





E1. At the prior: reconstruction 6.500, KL 0, total 6.500. Moving \mu to 1.5 with s = 1: the reconstruction term falls to (0 + 1)/0.5 = 2.000, the KL rises to \tfrac12 \cdot 1.5^2 = 1.125, total 3.125. Shrinking s, the blue dots gather around x; the reconstruction term falls towards 0 and the KL rises, slowly at first and then fast (the -\ln s^2 term).
E2. \mu = 1.200, s = 0.447: reconstruction 0.580, KL 1.125, total 1.705, as in the lecture. B6’s cloud (\mu = 1, s = 0.5) has total 1.818, a little higher.
E3. The KL term (3.622) dominates; the reconstruction term is tiny (0.005). A point-like cloud is very far from the prior in the KL sense, so the penalty keeps every cloud from collapsing; this is what keeps neighbouring images overlapping in latent space.
E4. With \beta = 5: \mu = 0.667, s = 0.745; the cloud moves towards the prior and widens. The reconstruction term (2.500) is now larger than \beta\timesKL (5 \times 0.294 = 1.469); total 3.969. With \beta = 0 the best cloud is a point at \mu = 1.5 (the readout gives s = 0.000): nothing pulls the clouds together, which is a plain autoencoder. Without the prior’s pull, the images are not spread over a known region, so we would not know where to draw new z from.
E5. At the prior: exact 6.500, from 20 draws 8.522. At the best cloud: exact 0.580, from the draws 0.806. Twenty random draws give a noisy estimate of an average. Training averages such estimates over many images and many steps, so the noise cancels out, much as one noisy measurement per step still leads downhill on average.

title: Exercise: the variational autoencoder
text:
Where this leads
The trained decoder can now be used on its own: draw z from the prior and decode to generate an image, walk from one z to another to interpolate, and use the reconstruction error to spot unusual images. That is the next unit.

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
About this lecture
A trained VAE gives us a decoder from a small latent space to images, and an encoder back. Today we use it.

Generate: draw z from the prior, decode.
Interpolate: walk in z from one image to another; the midpoint is not the pixel average.
Explore: what the latent space has learned about digits and about cell shapes.
Apply: denoising, anomaly detection, morphology spaces. And the limits: blurry images, nonsense far from the data.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Two trained VAEs, both 784 → 192 → 2 → 192 → 784, both run live in the demo: one on MNIST handwritten digits (adapted from the 3MB00A course), one on synthetic cell masks (four kinds: round, elongated, dividing, with a protrusion). The synthetic masks are honestly labelled as such; a VAE on real nucleus crops is the obvious next step and works the same way.

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
section: Generating: decode a draw from the prior
text:
Generating: decode a draw from the prior

Decoding a 15 \times 15 grid of points z \in [-3, 3]^2: almost every point gives a digit-like image, and neighbours are similar. Only the bottom middle, where no training digit lies, decodes to smudges. To make a new image: draw z \sim \mathcal N(0, I) and decode.

This is the classic picture of a 2D VAE. Point out: 0s on the left, 1s on the right and bottom right, 7s at the top, 6 and 5 between 0 and the middle, the crowded middle with 3, 8, 2, 9, 4. Between regions the images morph: a 7 becomes a 9, a 6 becomes a 0. The bottom middle (around z = (0, −2.5)) decodes to smudges: almost no digits are encoded there (1 of the 1000 test digits of the latent map has z₂ < −2 and |z₁| < 1), so the decoder was never trained there. The prior N(0, I) puts 86.5% of its draws inside radius 2 (1 − e^{−2}); the edges of this grid (|z| up to 3) are rarely drawn and decode to exaggerated versions of the outermost shapes.

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
Walking through latent space

Top: decode 7 equally spaced points on the line from the centre of the 1s to the centre of the 7s, z(t) = (1 - t)\,z_A + t\,z_B. Bottom: fade the two end images into each other, pixel by pixel, (1 - t)\,x_A + t\,x_B.

The latent walk passes through plausible shapes (here via a 9-like stroke).
The pixel fade is a double exposure: a faint 1 and a faint 7 on top of each other.


A straight line in latent space is a curve in pixel space, as with the moving spot in the autoencoder unit. The pixel average of two images is almost never an image of the same kind. The centres are the medians of the 1000 test-digit centres per class, as the demo’s “walk 1 → 7” preset uses: (2.46, 0.00) and (0.94, 1.21).

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
Midpoint vs average, by hand
A decoder that draws a bright bar on a 3-pixel image at position z: pixel i gets \max(0,\ 1 - |z - i|), i = 0, 1, 2.




z = 0
z = 1
z = 2




decoded
(1, 0, 0)
(0, 1, 0)
(0, 0, 1)




Latent midpoint of z = 0 and z = 2: z = 1, the bar in the middle, (0, 1, 0).
Pixel average of the two images: (0.5,\ 0,\ 0.5), two half-bright bars.

A linear decoder (PCA) would give the average; a curved decoder moves the bar.

This is the image version of the 3MB00A argument with a transient progenitor gene: the middle pixel is dark at both ends but bright at the midpoint. Ask the class for z = 0.5: (0.5, 0.5, 0): the bar halfway between pixels 0 and 1, smeared over both.

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
section: What the latent space has learned
text:
What the latent space has learned

Similar images are neighbours: in the digit VAE, 4 next to 9, and 3, 5, 8 together in the middle.
Two numbers are too few to keep ten digits apart: a vote among the 15 nearest test digits in z finds the right digit for 68% of test images.
The axes mean nothing by themselves: the KL penalty looks the same if the latent space is rotated, so “z_1” is not “thickness”. Read directions from decoded images, not from the axis labels.
Distances are only roughly meaningful, as in any nonlinear map.


The 68% is a leave-one-out 15-nearest-neighbour vote among the first 4000 MNIST test digits, computed with the demo’s weights. With a larger latent space (10–20 dimensions) the classes separate much better, but then we cannot draw the map. Contrast with PCA, where components are ordered by variance and orthogonal.

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
Try it: digits




Draw a digit and press Encode, or press “example ▸” for real MNIST test digits (20 of them, two of each). The cross is the cloud centre, the orange ellipse its ±2 sd. Drag z. Tick “decoded grid”. “walk 1 → 7” shows the latent walk. “sample from the prior” makes 7 new digits. “far outside” (3.3, −3.3) still decodes to a stroke: the decoder always answers, even where the prior almost never draws (density 0.00002 of that at 0).

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
section: Cell shapes: a morphology latent space
text:
Cell shapes: a morphology latent space




The same network trained on synthetic cell masks (28 \times 28): round, elongated, dividing, with a protrusion, at random sizes and orientations.

The map organises size (large round cells on the left), elongation and orientation (right) and dividing cells (bottom).
A walk in z is a smooth change of shape; a generated mask is a plausible new cell.
Thin protrusions are lost: two numbers cannot also hold their direction. Their reconstruction error is the highest of the four kinds.

A nonlinear relative of the point distribution model (PCA of landmark shapes), learned straight from pixels.


Synthetic data, made by the training script with a fixed seed (no external images): wobbly ellipses, dumbbells and discs with a thin bar. Mean squared pixel error of the reconstructions on 2000 test masks: 0.0129 overall; by kind round 0.0071, elongated 0.0113, dividing 0.0116, protrusion 0.0218. Real use: VAEs and related autoencoders on cell and nucleus images give “morphology spaces” in which drug treatments or cell states form regions (e.g. Ruan & Murphy 2019; Zaritsky et al. 2021). If the Shape models unit came first, compare: the point distribution model is linear and needs landmarks; the VAE is nonlinear and works on the mask directly.

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
Denoising




Columns: clean mask, with noise added (sd 0.3 per pixel), decoded from the code of the noisy mask.

The decoder can only draw cell-like images, so it cannot draw the noise.
Mean squared error against the clean mask: noisy input 0.045, 0.048, 0.047; decoded 0.009, 0.018, 0.016.
But it draws its own version of a cell: details the model never learned (a protrusion, a precise outline) are replaced by typical ones.

Denoising by “project onto what the model can draw”: the nonlinear cousin of keeping a few PCA components.


Rows are test masks 2 (round), 7 (dividing) and 11 (protrusion) of the demo’s examples, noise from a fixed seed as in the demo’s “noise on input” slider at 0.3. Not every case works: for example 4 (an elongated cell) the noisy code lands in the wrong place and the output error, 0.110, is worse than the noisy input’s 0.047. For the digit model the decoded image is usually worse than the noisy input in squared error (its reconstructions are already blurry), although it looks cleaner.

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
Anomaly detection

Top: input masks. Bottom: their reconstructions. Four normal test cells, then a ring, two cells and a square.

Normal cells (the 12 test examples of the demo): error 0.004–0.023. On 2000 test masks, 99% have error below 0.045.
Ring 0.172, two cells 0.253: far above, flagged as unusual. Their codes land far outside the prior’s circle.
Square 0.030: below the threshold. It is close enough to a round cell to be rebuilt as one. The detector only sees what the model cannot draw.


Errors are mean squared pixel errors between the mask and the decoded cloud centre, computed with the demo code. Reading: a threshold at the 99th percentile of normal errors flags about 1% of normal cells as false alarms (20 of 2000). In practice: flag unusual cells, out-of-focus images, debris or segmentation failures in a screen. The encoder centres: ring (−6.30, 3.49), two cells (−4.18, −0.36): both outside the plotted square of the demo, far in the prior’s tail.

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
Try it: cell shapes




“example ▸” steps through 12 test masks (three per kind) and then the three anomalies; the error is shown under the encoder input. Draw a filled blob to make your own cell (the brush is wide). Raise “noise on input” to see denoising. “walk round → dividing” morphs a round cell into a dividing one.

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
β-VAE: tidier space, blurrier images
Weight the KL more, \beta > 1:

Clouds are pulled harder to the prior: more overlap, a smoother latent space, and often directions that match one factor each (size, elongation, …): “disentangled”.
The decoder must serve wider clouds with one image each: blurrier, more average images.
\beta < 1: sharper reconstructions, but the gaps of a plain autoencoder start to return.

There is no free lunch: \beta trades image quality for latent-space quality.

Higgins et al. (2017), β-VAE: learning basic visual concepts with a constrained variational framework, ICLR. The elbo1d demo shows the same trade-off in one dimension: β = 5 pulls the best cloud from (1.2, 0.447) to (0.667, 0.745) and the reconstruction term rises from 0.58 to 2.5. Our two image VAEs were trained with β = 1.

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
Limits

Blurry outputs: the decoder outputs the average of all images that fit a given z (next slide). Fine detail and sharp edges are smeared.
Far from the data the decoder guesses: it always outputs an image, plausible or not. Generated images are only as good as the training images.
Small latent spaces lose detail (protrusions); large ones are hard to look at.
Sharper generators: GANs (a generator trained against a classifier that tries to tell real from fake) and diffusion models (learn to remove noise step by step, then start from pure noise). Both build on the same idea: a learned map from random numbers to images.

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
section: The math: why VAE images are blurry
text:
The math: why VAE images are blurry
Suppose several different images x are all encoded near the same z. The decoder outputs one image c for that z, chosen to minimise the expected squared error:
\mathbb E\big[\|x - c\|^2\big] = \|c - \mathbb E[x]\|^2 + \mathbb E\big[\|x - \mathbb E[x]\|^2\big] \quad\Rightarrow\quad c^* = \mathbb E[x \mid z].

The best output is the conditional mean: an average of sharp images is a blurry image.
The same holds for cross-entropy on pixel “ink”: the best ink probability is the average ink.
The wider the clouds (larger \beta), the more images share each z, and the blurrier the mean.

title: Generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
Summary







Idea
In one line




Generate
z \sim \mathcal N(0, I), decode


Interpolate
walk z(t) = (1-t)z_A + tz_B; the midpoint is a new shape, not a double exposure


Latent structure
similar images nearby; classes overlap in 2D; axes have no fixed meaning


Morphology space
a VAE on cell masks orders cells by size, elongation, division


Denoising
decode the code of a noisy image: only what the model can draw survives


Anomaly
high reconstruction error = unlike the training images (if the model cannot draw it)


Limits
blurry (conditional mean), unreliable far from the data; GANs and diffusion go further

title: Quiz: segmentation as energy minimisation
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Throughout, labels are 1 (object) and 0 (background), and the energy is E(L) = \sum_p D_p(L_p) + \lambda \sum_{(p,q)} w_{pq}[L_p \ne L_q].

Q1. Why does thresholding a noisy image give isolated wrong pixels, and why does the smoothness term remove them?






Hint





What information does thresholding use for one pixel? What does an isolated pixel cost in the smoothness term?









Answer





Thresholding looks at each pixel’s own intensity only. With noise, some background pixels are brighter than the threshold (and some object pixels darker), and nothing stops them from getting the wrong label. An isolated wrong pixel disagrees with all 4 neighbours, which costs 4\lambda (with w = 1). Flipping it removes that cost and adds only the difference of its data costs, which is small for a pixel close to the threshold. So for large enough \lambda it flips.




Q2. Background pixels are \mathcal N(40, s^2) and object pixels \mathcal N(200, s^2), and D_p(\ell) = -\log P(I_p \mid \ell). At which grey level does \lambda = 0 put the threshold? Does it depend on s?






Hint





Set D_p(0) = D_p(1). The normalising constants of the two Gaussians are equal.









Answer





(I - 40)^2 = (I - 200)^2 gives I = 120, halfway between the means. It does not depend on s, as long as both classes have the same s. With different widths, or with a prior that one class is more common, the crossing point moves.




Q3. What do \lambda = 0 and a very large \lambda give?






Hint





Which term dominates in each case?









Answer





\lambda = 0: only the data term counts, each pixel takes its cheaper label: plain thresholding. Very large \lambda: any boundary costs more than the data can save, so the minimum has no boundary: all pixels get the same label, whichever has the smaller total data cost.




Q4. In a 1D profile, a real structure is 2 samples wide and each of its samples saves 3 units of data cost when labelled object. Above which \lambda does the optimal labelling remove it?






Hint





Keeping it inside the background costs two boundaries.









Answer





Keeping it saves 2 \cdot 3 = 6 in data and costs 2 boundaries, 2\lambda. It disappears when 2\lambda > 6, i.e. \lambda > 3. Thin structures are the first casualties of a large \lambda: their data gain grows with their area, their boundary cost does not shrink.




Q5. How many labellings does a 512 \times 512 image have? Why is that not a problem on a single row of pixels?






Hint





On a row, the best labelling of the first k pixels only depends on the label of pixel k.









Answer





2^{262144}, far beyond enumeration. On a row (a chain), dynamic programming keeps only two numbers per pixel, C_k(0) and C_k(1), the best energy of the first k pixels ending in each label. Each step looks at the previous two, so the cost is O(n). On a 2D grid, a pixel has neighbours in several directions that are linked through loops, and this bookkeeping breaks down.




Q6. Show that -\log of P(L \mid I) \propto P(I \mid L)\,P(L) gives E(L) when P(I \mid L) = \prod_p P(I_p \mid L_p) and P(L) \propto \exp(-\lambda \sum w_{pq}[L_p \ne L_q]).






Hint





\log turns products into sums.









Answer





-\log P(L \mid I) = -\sum_p \log P(I_p \mid L_p) + \lambda \sum w_{pq}[L_p \ne L_q] + \text{const} = \sum_p D_p(L_p) + \lambda\sum w_{pq}[L_p \ne L_q] + \text{const}. The constant (normalisation) does not depend on L, so the most probable labelling is the one with the smallest energy.




Q7. The smoothness term uses w_{pq} = 1 for every pair of neighbours. What would you change to make the boundary prefer to follow the edges of the object?






Hint





Where should a boundary be cheap?









Answer





Make w_{pq} small where the intensities of p and q differ a lot, for example w_{pq} = \exp\!\big(-(I_p - I_q)^2/2\sigma^2\big). A boundary between two very different pixels is then almost free, and the minimum-energy boundary is pulled onto the image edges. This is the weight used in graph-cut segmentation.

title: Exercise: segmentation as energy minimisation
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Labelling
L_p = 1 (object) or 0 (background) for every pixel p


Data term
D_p(\ell): the cost of label \ell at pixel p; here D_p(\ell) = (I_p - \mu_\ell)^2 / 2s^2, i.e. -\log of a Gaussian


Smoothness term
\lambda \sum_{(p,q)} w_{pq}[L_p \ne L_q]; in this exercise w_{pq} = 1, so it is \lambda times the number of boundaries


Energy
E(L) = data term + smoothness term; the segmentation is the labelling with the smallest E


Thresholding
the minimum for \lambda = 0: every pixel takes its cheaper label


Dynamic programming
on a chain: C_k(\ell) = D_k(\ell) + \min\big(C_{k-1}(\ell),\, C_{k-1}(1-\ell) + \lambda\big)



Labellings of a row are written as strings, for example 11010.

title: Exercise: segmentation as energy minimisation
text:
By hand
A 1 \times 5 image I = (3, 3, 1, 3, 0) with \mu_0 = 0 and \mu_1 = 3. For B1–B3 take D_p(\ell) = (I_p - \mu_\ell)^2 (that is, 2s^2 = 1).
B1. Write down D_p(0) and D_p(1) for the five pixels. Which labelling does thresholding give?
B2. Compute the data term, the number of boundaries and the energy of the four labellings (a) 11010, (b) 11110, (c) 11111, (d) 00000, for \lambda = 1 and for \lambda = 5. Which of the four is best in each case? Find the values of \lambda at which the winner changes.
B3. Fill in the dynamic-programming table C_k(0), C_k(1), k = 1, \dots, 5, for \lambda = 2. What is the minimum energy, and which labelling achieves it? (Keep track of which choice wins at each step, and trace back from the end.)
B4. The demo below uses \mu_0 = 60, \mu_1 = 160 and s = 30, so D_p(\ell) = (I_p - \mu_\ell)^2 / 1800. (a) At which grey level is the threshold? (b) Its thin structure consists of two samples with grey levels 140 and 221, with background on both sides. Compute D(0) and D(1) for both. Above which \lambda does the optimal labelling drop the structure?
B5. In a 2D image (4-neighbours, w_{pq} = 1), a single pixel of grey level 120 is surrounded by background pixels that are clearly background. Use the model of B4. What does thresholding do with it? Above which \lambda does the optimal labelling call it background?
B6. Predict: suppose we know the object is rare, only 20% of the pixels, and include that in the data term, D_p(\ell) = -\log\big(\pi_\ell\, P(I_p \mid \ell)\big) with \pi_1 = 0.2, \pi_0 = 0.8. Does the threshold for \lambda = 0 move up or down? Why does that make sense?
B7 (math). Show that with the prior of B6 the threshold for \lambda = 0 is \tfrac12(\mu_0 + \mu_1) + \dfrac{s^2 \log(\pi_0/\pi_1)}{\mu_1 - \mu_0}, and evaluate it for the model of B4.






Solutions





B1. D(0) = I^2 = 9, 9, 1, 9, 0 and D(1) = (3 - I)^2 = 0, 0, 4, 0, 9. Thresholding takes the cheaper label at every pixel: 11010 (the dark pixel 3 and pixel 5 are background).

Then, writing C_k = \big(C_k(0), C_k(1)\big): C_2(0) = 9 + \min(9, 0 + 2) = 11, C_2(1) = 0 + \min(0, 9 + 2) = 0; C_3(0) = 1 + \min(11, 0 + 2) = 3, C_3(1) = 4 + \min(0, 11 + 2) = 4; C_4(0) = 9 + \min(3, 4 + 2) = 12, C_4(1) = 0 + \min(4, 3 + 2) = 4; C_5(0) = 0 + \min(12, 4 + 2) = 6, C_5(1) = 9 + \min(4, 12 + 2) = 13. The minimum is C_5(0) = 6. Trace back: C_5(0) came from C_4(1); C_4(1) from C_3(1); C_3(1) from C_2(1); C_2(1) from C_1(1). The labelling is 11110, with data 4 and one boundary: 4 + 2 = 6, as in B2.
B4. (a) \tfrac12(60 + 160) = 110. (b) Grey level 140: D(0) = 80^2/1800 = 3.556, D(1) = 20^2/1800 = 0.222. Grey level 221: D(0) = 161^2/1800 = 14.401, D(1) = 61^2/1800 = 2.067. Labelling both as object instead of background saves (3.556 + 14.401) - (0.222 + 2.067) = 15.667 in data, and costs 2 boundaries. The structure is dropped when 2\lambda > 15.667, i.e. for \lambda > 7.83.

B6. The threshold moves up, towards the brighter, rarer class: the object label now carries an extra cost -\log 0.2 > -\log 0.8, so a pixel must look more clearly like an object before we call it one. For the model of B4 it moves from 110 to 122.5 (B7).
B7. Set D_p(0) = D_p(1): \frac{(I - \mu_0)^2}{2s^2} - \log\pi_0 = \frac{(I - \mu_1)^2}{2s^2} - \log\pi_1. For B4: 110 + 900 \cdot \log 4 / 100 = 110 + 12.5 = 122.5.

title: Exercise: segmentation as energy minimisation
text:
Explore
The demo shows a noisy line profile of 80 samples across a cell (samples 13–50) and a thin bright structure (samples 65–66). The dashed lines are the two levels \mu_0 and \mu_1, the dotted line the threshold halfway between them. Below the plot, three strips: the true labels, thresholding (\lambda = 0), and the labelling with the smallest energy for the chosen \lambda, computed exactly by dynamic programming. Black dots mark wrong samples. The table gives the energy of both labellings. The \lambda slider is finer at small values.



E1. Press λ = 0: threshold. How many samples are wrong, and how many boundaries are there? Then press λ = 3. Compare the data terms of the two labellings: which is larger, and why is the optimal labelling still the better one?
E2. Starting from \lambda = 0, move the slider up slowly. At which \lambda do all wrong samples disappear? At which \lambda is the thin structure lost? Compare with B4.
E3. Press too smooth (\lambda = 100). How many boundaries are left, and which samples are now wrong? Why does the background on the left become object, rather than the cell becoming background?
E4. Set the noise to 60 (with \lambda = 3). How many samples are wrong with thresholding, and with the optimal labelling? Try other values of \lambda: can you find one that gets most of the profile right? What do you lose?
E5. Reset, then lower \mu_1 to 110 (keep \lambda = 3). What happens to the threshold and to the errors? What does this say about the intensity model?






Solutions





E1. Thresholding: 3 wrong samples (sample 45, a dark sample inside the cell, becomes background; samples 52 and 74, bright noise in the background, become object), 10 boundaries, energy 40.4 (all data, since \lambda = 0). At \lambda = 3: data 47.3 for the optimal labelling against 40.4 for thresholding: it pays more in data, because some samples now take their more expensive label. But it has only 4 boundaries instead of 10, so its total is 47.3 + 12 = 59.3, against 40.4 + 30 = 70.4 for thresholding. And it has 0 wrong samples.
E2. On the slider: at \lambda = 0.5 one error is gone (2 wrong, 8 boundaries), at \lambda = 1.5 only 1 is wrong, and from \lambda = 1.75 there are no wrong samples (4 boundaries). The thin structure survives up to \lambda = 7.75 and is lost at \lambda = 8 (2 boundaries, 2 wrong samples): B4 predicted the switch at 7.83.
E3. One boundary is left, between samples 50 and 51, and 14 samples are wrong: the 12 background samples on the left and the 2 samples of the thin structure. One boundary must stay, because labelling everything background (data 258.0) or everything object (248.9) costs more than 122.7 + 100. With one boundary, the cheaper way is to give the 12 dark samples on the left the object label (they cost 59.7 more data) and save the boundary at the left edge of the cell (100). This happens for \lambda above about 59.7 (on the slider from 59.75).
E4. With noise 60, thresholding gets 21 samples wrong (31 boundaries); the optimal labelling at \lambda = 3 gets 9 wrong (9 boundaries). The best on the slider is \lambda = 6.25 to 8.75: 5 wrong samples and 4 boundaries. The cell and the thin structure are both found, but the boundaries are off: the cell starts one sample early and ends three samples late, and the thin structure is one sample too wide. From \lambda = 9 the thin structure is gone (6 wrong). With this much noise, the smoothness term can remove the specks, but it cannot place the boundaries exactly: the data near a boundary are too noisy to say where it is.
E5. The threshold moves to \tfrac12(60 + 110) = 85. Thresholding now gets 10 samples wrong (bright noise in the background passes the low threshold), and the optimal labelling at \lambda = 3 still gets 5 wrong: the cell and the thin structure come out too wide, because background samples next to them now look like object. The smoothness term helps, but it cannot fix a wrong intensity model: the data term says the wrong thing everywhere. The model (\mu_0, \mu_1, s) has to fit the image; in the graph-cut unit it is estimated from seed pixels.

title: Exercise: segmentation as energy minimisation
text:
Where this leads
On a chain, dynamic programming finds the exact minimum. On a 2D image, the same energy with two labels can still be minimised exactly, by turning it into a minimum cut of a graph: the next two units. The weights w_{pq} then depend on the image, so that boundaries prefer to follow edges.

title: Quantisation and bit depth
text:
About this lecture

A digital image loses information twice: where it is measured (sampling) and which values it can store (quantisation).
How many grey levels b bits give, and what rounding to them does: banding, and an error of predictable size.
Dithering: why adding noise on purpose makes an image look better.
How the error shrinks with each extra bit: about 6 dB per bit.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

The images lecture said “typically 8 or 16 bits”. This lecture asks what that choice costs and when it matters. The plan: picture and demo first, the variance formula afterwards. The next unit (camera noise) asks how many bits the measurement itself can fill, and owns the noise models, SNR and PSNR; this lecture’s SNR is only the rounding one.

text:
Two ways to lose information
A camera measures a continuous brightness f(x, y) and stores a matrix of whole numbers:









Sampling

title: Quantisation and bit depth
text:
Bits and levels
With b bits a pixel can take 2^b values, 0, 1, \dots, 2^b - 1:



bits b

levels 2^b
2

Spread over the same range (say black to white), the step between neighbouring levels is \Delta = \text{range}/(2^b - 1).
One more bit → twice as many levels → half the step.
8 bits: the step is 1/255 of the range. 12 bits: 1/4095, a 16 times finer step.

title: Quantisation and bit depth
text:
Try it: quantise an image




Start on the ramp at 4 bits: 16 visible bands. Slide the bits down to 1 and up to 8; at 6 bits most people stop seeing bands on a projector. Point at the error image: a sawtooth, between −Δ/2 and +Δ/2, and the histogram is flat. Then “4 bits: banding” on the smooth blobs: contour lines appear that are not in the scene. Then “4 bits + dither”: the bands are gone, replaced by fine grain, and the histogram becomes a triangle. Then the micrograph at 2 bits with error diffusion: only 4 grey levels, but it still looks like the cell.

title: Quantisation and bit depth
section: What the rounding error looks like
text:
What the rounding error looks like

Rounding moves each value to the nearest level, so the error is between −Δ/2 and +Δ/2.
In a smooth region the error is a sawtooth: the image jumps in steps of \Delta where it should change gradually. The eye sees the jumps as contour lines: banding (posterisation).
In a busy or noisy region, the error looks like random noise, evenly spread between −Δ/2 and +Δ/2.
Its typical size is about 0.29\,\Delta (root mean square). The demo’s readout shows it: at 4 bits, RMS error 0.0192 of the range.
One more bit halves the error. In decibels: about 6 dB per bit.

title: Quantisation and bit depth
section: The math: the error of rounding
text:
The math: the error of rounding
Model the error e as uniform on [-\Delta/2, \Delta/2], with density 1/\Delta. Then
\mathbb E[e] = 0, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(e) = \int_{-\Delta/2}^{\Delta/2} e^2\,\frac{1}{\Delta}\,de = \frac{1}{\Delta}\left[\frac{e^3}{3}\right]_{-\Delta/2}^{\Delta/2} = \frac{\Delta^2}{12}.
So \text{RMS} = \Delta/\sqrt{12} \approx 0.289\,\Delta. Here the signal-to-noise ratio in decibels compares variances: \text{SNR} = 10\log_{10}(\sigma^2_\text{signal}/\sigma^2_\text{noise}) (SNR and PSNR in general: camera-noise unit). For a signal spread evenly over the full range R = (2^b - 1)\Delta, \sigma^2_\text{signal} = R^2/12, so
\text{SNR} = 10\log_{10}\,(2^b - 1)^2 \approx 20\,b\log_{10}2 \approx 6.02\,b \text{ dB}.
(For a full-scale sine wave, the textbook value is 6.02\,b + 1.76 dB.) The model holds when the signal changes by many steps across the image; on a perfectly flat region the error is one constant number, not noise.

title: Quantisation and bit depth
text:
Dithering: add noise before rounding
Rounding a smooth gradient gives bands, because many neighbouring pixels round the same way.

Random dither: add a little noise (up to ±Δ/2) to every pixel before rounding. A pixel 75 % of the way from one level to the next now rounds up 75 % of the time. On average, the grey value is right.
The bands turn into fine grain. The total error is a bit larger (a triangle instead of a box, RMS \times\sqrt2), but it no longer follows the image, and the eye averages grain away.
Error diffusion (Floyd–Steinberg): round a pixel, then pass its error on to the neighbours not yet visited. The local average stays right. This is how a printer shows grey with only black ink.

title: Quantisation and bit depth
section: The math: why random dither is unbiased
text:
The math: why random dither is unbiased
Measure in units of \Delta, write a value as x = k + f with k an integer and 0 \le f < 1, and add u uniform on [-\tfrac12, \tfrac12). Then x + u rounds up to k + 1 exactly when u \ge \tfrac12 - f, which has probability f:
\mathbb E[\operatorname{round}(x + u)] = (1 - f)\,k + f\,(k + 1) = k + f = x.
No bias, for every x: the expected output is a straight line, not a staircase. The price: the error is 1 - f with probability f and -f with probability 1 - f, so \mathbb E[e^2] = f(1-f); averaged over f, \int_0^1 f(1-f)\,df = \tfrac16. So the error variance is \Delta^2/6, twice that of plain rounding.

title: Quantisation and bit depth
text:
Summary

b bits give 2^b levels; rounding to them makes an error of at most half a step (typically 0.29 steps): about 6 dB per bit.
In smooth regions the error shows as banding; dithering trades the bands for fine, unbiased noise.
Next: where the numbers come from. A camera counts electrons, and the count is noisy: how many bits are worth storing?

title: Quiz: principal component analysis
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Why do we subtract the mean image before looking for the direction of largest spread?






Answer





We want the directions in which the images differ from each other. Without centring, the best direction through (0, 0) mostly points at the mean image: it describes how bright the images are on average, which one number (the mean) already tells us.




Q2. Two-pixel images from neighbouring pixels of a smooth image: where do PC1 and PC2 point, and what do their scores measure?






Answer





PC1 \approx (1, 1)/\sqrt2: both pixels together, the score measures the brightness of the pair. PC2 \approx (1, -1)/\sqrt2: one up, the other down, the score measures the difference, a small edge. Neighbouring pixels are similar, so PC1 carries most of the variance.




Q3. A covariance matrix is S = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}. Give the principal components, their variances, and the share of PC1.






Hint





For \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix} the eigenvectors are (1, \pm 1)/\sqrt2.









Answer





PC1 = (1, 1)/\sqrt2 with variance 3 + 1 = 4; PC2 = (1, -1)/\sqrt2 with variance 3 - 1 = 2. Share of PC1: 4/6 = 67\,\%. The total, 6, is also the sum of the diagonal.




Q4. Mean image (0.6, 0.6), PC1 = (1, 1)/\sqrt2. Encode the image (0.9, 0.5) with one score, rebuild it, and give the squared error.






Answer





Centred: (0.3, -0.1). Score (0.3 - 0.1)/\sqrt2 = 0.141. Rebuilt: (0.6, 0.6) + 0.141\cdot(1, 1)/\sqrt2 = (0.7, 0.7). Error (0.2, -0.2), squared length 0.08: the difference between the two pixels is lost.




Q5. The eigenvalues of a PCA are 6, 2, 1, 0.5, 0.5. How many components do you need for 90 % of the variance? What is the mean squared reconstruction error with that many?






Answer





Cumulative shares: 60, 80, 90, 95, 100 %. Three components give exactly 90 %. The error is the sum of the dropped eigenvalues: 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.




Q6. Both the Fourier transform and PCA rewrite an image patch in a new orthonormal basis. What is the main difference?






Answer





The Fourier basis (waves) is fixed: the same for every image. The PCA basis is learned from a set of images: the eigenvectors of their covariance, ordered by how much those images vary along them. For a given number of kept coefficients PCA has the smallest squared error on its own data; Fourier is general and needs no fitting. On ordinary image patches the two look alike.




Q7. You run PCA on cell measurements: diameter in nm and circularity (between 0 and 1). PC1 explains 99.99 % of the variance. What has gone wrong?






Answer





Probably nothing about the cells: the diameter in nm has a numerically huge variance compared with a number between 0 and 1, so PC1 is just “diameter”. PCA depends on the units. Standardise each feature (divide by its standard deviation) when the features have different units.




Q8. (math) Why is the variance of the scores along a unit vector \mathbf u equal to \mathbf u^\top S\mathbf u, and why is it largest at an eigenvector of S?






Answer





The scores are \mathbf u^\top\mathbf y_i (centred, mean 0), so their variance is \frac1n\sum(\mathbf u^\top\mathbf y_i)^2 = \mathbf u^\top\big(\frac1n\sum\mathbf y_i\mathbf y_i^\top\big)\mathbf u = \mathbf u^\top S\mathbf u. Writing \mathbf u = \sum c_j\mathbf u_j in the orthonormal eigenbasis, \mathbf u^\top S\mathbf u = \sum\lambda_j c_j^2 with \sum c_j^2 = 1: a weighted average of the eigenvalues, largest when all the weight is on \lambda_1, that is \mathbf u = \mathbf u_1.
