correct; decide later what to do with negatives



Same trap when averaging: in uint16, (40\,000 + 30\,000)/2 gives 2232 instead of 35 000, because the sum wraps before the division.

title: 12- and 16-bit images in practice
section: The math: wrap-around is arithmetic modulo 2^n
text:
The math: wrap-around is arithmetic modulo 2^n
An n-bit unsigned integer stores every result modulo 2^n:
a \ominus b = (a - b) \bmod 2^n, \qquad 150 \ominus 160 = -10 + 65\,536 = 65\,526.
Two’s complement uses the same rule to store negatives: -x is stored as 2^n - x. That is why addition and subtraction circuits do not care whether a number is signed: only the interpretation of the top half of the range differs (2^{n-1} \dots 2^n - 1 means -2^{n-1} \dots -1).
Saturation is \min(\max(a - b, 0), 2^n - 1): not modular, and not linear either; \mathbb E[\max(X, 0)] > \mathbb E[X] when X has noise around 0.

title: 12- and 16-bit images in practice
text:
Rules for arithmetic

Compute in a wider type: convert to float (or int32) before subtracting, adding, averaging, filtering. A filter with negative weights needs signed results anyway.
Convert back on purpose, with an explicit scale and clip, and only for storage or display.
Watch the conventions: some programs scale floats to [0, 1], others keep raw counts. Converting 4095 (uint16) to a “[0, 1] float” can give 4095/65\,535 \approx 0.0625, not 1.
Summing frames: 16 frames of a 12-bit camera fit in uint16 (16 \cdot 4095 = 65\,520); the 17th does not.

title: 12- and 16-bit images in practice
section: Showing 12–16 bits on an 8-bit screen: windows
text:
Showing 12–16 bits on an 8-bit screen: windows
A window [\ell, h] maps raw values linearly to the 256 display levels and clips the rest:

v \le \ell → black, v \ge h → white, in between a linear ramp.
Window/level: width W = h - \ell, centre L = (\ell + h)/2.
A narrow window spreads a small range of values over all display levels: more contrast, more clipping.
Auto-contrast: set \ell and h to percentiles (say 0.5 % and 99.5 %), so a few saturated or dead pixels do not set the scale.

The window changes only the display. Measure on the raw values.

title: 12- and 16-bit images in practice
text:
The math: the window formula
The display level of a raw value v is the straight line through (\ell, 0) and (h, 255), clipped and rounded:
d(v) = \operatorname{round}\!\left(255 \cdot \operatorname{clip}\!\left(\frac{v - \ell}{h - \ell},\; 0,\; 1\right)\right).
With width W = h - \ell, one display level covers W/256 raw values: for W = 4096, 16 raw values share one grey on screen. A LUT (look-up table) generalises this: any function from raw value to colour, stored as a table. The window is the linear LUT.

title: 12- and 16-bit images in practice
text:
CT: Hounsfield units and windows
CT measures X-ray attenuation \mu and reports it relative to water, in Hounsfield units (HU): air −1000, fat ≈ −100, water 0, soft tissue 20–80, bone several hundred to 2000+.
Soft tissue differs by tens of HU, but the image spans 4000 HU: no single window shows everything. Radiologists switch between standard windows:

Files often store HU + 1024 as unsigned numbers, with the offset in the header; forget it and every window is 1024 HU off.

title: 12- and 16-bit images in practice
text:
The math: Hounsfield units
\text{HU} = 1000 \cdot \frac{\mu - \mu_\text{water}}{\mu_\text{water} - \mu_\text{air}}.
Water is 0 and air is −1000 by construction; one HU is 0.1 % of the attenuation of water. A stored value s becomes HU through a linear rescale, \text{HU} = a\,s + c (often a = 1, c = -1024), recorded in the file header.

title: 12- and 16-bit images in practice
text:
Try it: CT windows


Synthetic slice: body, fat layer, lungs with vessels, a vertebra at the back, an organ between the lungs with a faint lesion 20 HU brighter than its surroundings. Soft tissue: organs visible, lungs black, bone white. Lung: vessels in the lung, everything else white. Bone: the cortical rim. Narrow W150 L70: the lesion appears. Then “uint16 HU+1024” with the soft-tissue preset: everything white, because the window was meant for HU, not for stored numbers.

title: 12- and 16-bit images in practice
section: Colour maps, HDR and tone mapping
text:
Colour maps, HDR and tone mapping

A LUT can map grey values to colours. A “hi-lo” LUT marks clipped pixels (blue below, red above): use it to set a window honestly. Perceptual colour maps are on the colour day.
High dynamic range (HDR) scenes span 10^5 : 1 or more. A linear window either loses the shadows or the highlights.
Tone mapping compresses the range with a non-linear curve (e.g. logarithmic, or x/(1 + x)), globally or adapted to the neighbourhood. Good for looking, bad for measuring: it changes the ratios between pixels.

title: 12- and 16-bit images in practice
text:
Summary

12-bit data in a 16-bit container look black when shown as 0…65 535: the display range, not the data, is wrong.
Integer arithmetic wraps (modulo 2^n) or saturates; both are wrong for negative results. Compute in float or a wider type.
A window maps a range of raw values to the 256 display levels; CT uses standard windows in Hounsfield units.
Displays, LUTs and tone mapping are for looking; analysis uses the raw numbers.

title: Quiz: graph-cut segmentation
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. The graph has one node per pixel, s = object, t = background; t-links s \to p with capacity D_p(0) and p \to t with D_p(1); n-links \lambda w_{pq} in both directions.

Q1. A pixel ends up on the source side of the cut. Which of its t-links is cut, and what does that cost correspond to?






Hint





Only edges from S to T count.









Answer





p \in S means L_p = 1 (object). The edge p \to t goes from S to T and is cut, at cost D_p(1): the data cost of labelling p object. The edge s \to p lies inside S and costs nothing.




Q2. Why is each n-link added in both directions?






Hint





Which pixel of a disagreeing pair is on the source side?









Answer





The boundary cost \lambda w_{pq} must be paid whether p is object and q background, or the other way round. With p \in S, q \in T the edge p \to q is cut; with q \in S, p \in T the edge q \to p is. Exactly one of the two counts, so the cut pays \lambda w_{pq} once.




Q3. Two neighbours have grey levels 100 and 160, and \sigma = 20. What is w_{pq}? What if they were 100 and 105?






Hint





w_{pq} = \exp(-(I_p - I_q)^2/2\sigma^2).









Answer





60^2/(2 \cdot 400) = 4.5, so w = e^{-4.5} = 0.011: a boundary there is almost free. For 100 and 105: 25/800 = 0.031, w = e^{-0.031} = 0.97: almost the full cost.




Q4. How does an object seed force a pixel to be object? Why not simply set its label after the cut?






Hint





A seed also affects its neighbours.









Answer





Its t-link s \to p gets a capacity larger than any cut could cost (and p \to t capacity 0), so no minimum cut puts it on the background side. Setting the label afterwards would not do the same: the seed must take part in the optimisation, so that its neighbours, through the n-links, are pulled towards the object label too.




Q5. Why does a graph cut with a large \lambda tend to remove thin structures, but keep large blobs with the same intensity?






Hint





Compare how data gain and boundary cost grow with size.









Answer





The data gain of keeping a structure grows with its area, the boundary cost with its perimeter. A thin line of length \ell has area \ell and perimeter about 2\ell: its gain per unit boundary is small. A disk of radius r has area \pi r^2 and perimeter 2\pi r: the gain per unit boundary grows with r. This preference for short boundaries is the shrinking bias.




Q6. Segmented with a 4-neighbourhood, a round cell comes out with flat sides and diagonal corners cut off. Why, and what helps?






Hint





How much does a diagonal boundary cost per unit length with 4 neighbours?









Answer





With 4 neighbours the boundary cost is the city-block length: a diagonal boundary costs \sqrt2 \approx 1.41 times as much per unit of true length as a horizontal or vertical one. The cut therefore prefers axis-aligned boundaries (metrication). An 8-neighbourhood with suitable weights (here \tfrac12 for sides and \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt2} for diagonals) makes the cost nearly the same in every direction.




Q7. Object seeds are placed on a nucleus and background seeds only on the white space around the cell. The result includes the cytoplasm. Why, and how do you fix it?






Hint





What does the intensity model learn from these seeds?









Answer





The model only knows “nucleus grey” (object) and “white” (background). The cytoplasm is grey too, so its data term says object, and nothing in the energy says otherwise. Add background seeds on the cytoplasm: the background model then includes its grey levels, and where nucleus and cytoplasm overlap in intensity, the seeds and the contrast weights at the nuclear envelope decide.




Q8. Can a graph cut minimise an energy that rewards boundaries, V(L_p, L_q) = -[L_p \ne L_q]?






Hint





Check the submodularity condition V(0,1) + V(1,0) \ge V(0,0) + V(1,1).









Answer





No: V(0,1) + V(1,0) = -2 < 0 = V(0,0) + V(1,1), so it is not submodular. The n-links would need negative capacity, and adding a constant does not help because it does not depend on whether the labels differ. Such energies are NP-hard in general (maximum cut).

title: Exercise: graph-cut segmentation
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Nodes
one per pixel, plus s (object) and t (background)


t-links
s \to p with capacity D_p(0), p \to t with capacity D_p(1)


n-links
p \to q and q \to p, each with capacity \lambda w_{pq}, for 4-neighbours p, q


Labelling from a cut
L_p = 1 (object) if p is on the source side, else 0


Cut = energy
c(S, T) = \sum_p D_p(L_p) + \lambda \sum w_{pq}[L_p \ne L_q] = E(L)


Contrast weights
w_{pq} = \exp\!\big(-(I_p - I_q)^2/2\sigma^2\big); \sigma = \infty means w_{pq} = 1


Seeds
an object seed gets s \to p with infinite capacity; a background seed p \to t



Throughout, grey levels are 0 to 3 with \mu_0 = 0, \mu_1 = 3 and D_p(\ell) = (I_p - \mu_\ell)^2, so D_p(0) = I_p^2 and D_p(1) = (3 - I_p)^2. This is what the first demo uses.

title: Exercise: graph-cut segmentation
text:
By hand
B1. The 1 \times 3 image I = (3, 1, 3), with w_{pq} = 1. (a) Draw the graph: 5 nodes, 6 t-links, 2 pairs of n-links. Write every capacity for \lambda = 1. (b) List all 8 cuts (labellings) with their cost. Which is the minimum? Which labelling does thresholding give? (c) Repeat (b) for \lambda = 2. At which \lambda does the minimum change?
B2. Same image, now with contrast weights, \sigma = 1. (a) Compute w_{12} and w_{23}. What is w_{pq} for a grey-level difference of 1, and of 3? (b) Compute the energy of 101 and 111 for \lambda = 2 and \lambda = 5. Up to which \lambda does the dark pixel stay background? (c) Is that what you want if the dark pixel is noise? If it is a real gap between two objects?
B3. The 2 \times 2 image \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, 4-neighbours (4 pairs of n-links), w_{pq} = 1, \lambda = 2. Write labellings as top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right, e.g. 1100 = top row object. (a) Give the t-link capacities of the four pixels. (b) Compute the cost of the cuts 1100, 1000, 1110, 1111 and 0000. Then argue (or check by listing all 16) which cut is the minimum.
B4. Same 2 \times 2 image and \lambda, but the bottom-left pixel (grey level 1) is an object seed. Which capacities change? What is the minimum cut now, and its cost (counting the seed’s data cost D(1) = 4)?
B5. Shrinking bias. A 6 \times 6 image is 0 everywhere except column 2, which is a vertical line of grey level 2, and columns 4–6, a band of grey level 2 that touches the right border. Use w_{pq} = 1. (a) How much data cost does the line save by being object rather than background? How many n-links does labelling it object cut? Above which \lambda does the minimum drop the line? (b) The same for the band. (Its right side lies on the image border: no n-links there.) (c) Generalise: a long strip of width k pixels and data gain g per pixel. Above which \lambda is it removed?
B6. Metrication. Consider a long straight boundary in a large image with w_{pq} = 1. (a) With 4-neighbours, how many n-links does a horizontal boundary of length \ell cut? And a 45° staircase boundary of the same Euclidean length? (b) With 8-neighbours, horizontal and vertical n-links get weight \tfrac12, diagonal ones \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}. Compute the cost per unit length of a horizontal and of a 45° boundary. (c) Which neighbourhood gives the more “round” results, and why?
B7 (math). Show that the pairwise term V(L_p, L_q) = \lambda w_{pq}[L_p \ne L_q] with \lambda w_{pq} \ge 0 satisfies V(0,1) + V(1,0) \ge V(0,0) + V(1,1). Which pairwise term in a segmentation energy would violate it?






Solutions





B1. (a) D(0) = 9, 1, 9 and D(1) = 0, 4, 0: t-links s \to 1: 9, s \to 2: 1, s \to 3: 9; 1 \to t: 0, 2 \to t: 4, 3 \to t: 0. n-links 1 \leftrightarrow 2 and 2 \leftrightarrow 3: capacity \lambda = 1 each way. (b) Writing data + boundaries:

At \lambda = 1 the minimum is 101 (cost 3), the same as thresholding. (c) At \lambda = 2 the minimum is 111 (cost 4). 101 costs 1 + 2\lambda, 111 costs 4: they tie at \lambda = 1.5.
B2. (a) w_{12} = w_{23} = e^{-2^2/2} = e^{-2} = 0.135. For a difference of 1: e^{-0.5} = 0.607; of 3: e^{-4.5} = 0.011. (b) E(101) = 1 + \lambda \cdot 2 \cdot 0.135: 1.541 at \lambda = 2, 2.353 at \lambda = 5. E(111) = 4. The dark pixel stays background as long as 1 + 0.271\lambda < 4, i.e. up to \lambda = 11.08. (c) Contrast weights make a boundary across a large intensity jump almost free. That protects a real gap between two objects, but it also protects a noise pixel that differs strongly from its neighbours. \sigma should be larger than typical noise differences and smaller than the jumps at real edges.
B3. (a) Grey levels 3, 2, 1, 0: s \to p: 9, 4, 1, 0; p \to t: 0, 1, 4, 9. (b) 1100: data 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 2, n-links cut: top-left–bottom-left and top-right–bottom-right, 2, cost 2 + 2 \cdot 2 = 6. 1000: data 0 + 4 + 1 + 0 = 5, 2 n-links, cost 9. 1110: data 0 + 1 + 4 + 0 = 5, 2 n-links, cost 9. 1111: data 0 + 1 + 4 + 9 = 14, cost 14. 0000: data 9 + 4 + 1 + 0 = 14, cost 14. The minimum is 1100 with cost 6: it has the smallest possible data cost (each pixel takes its cheaper label, total 2), and any labelling with both labels cuts at least 2 n-links, so no labelling with a boundary can beat 2 + 4 = 6; the two without a boundary cost 14. Listing all 16 confirms it; the next best are 1000 and 1110 (9).
B4. The seed’s t-links become s \to p: \infty, p \to t: 0 (and its data cost D(1) = 4 is paid in any allowed labelling). Only labellings with bottom-left = 1 are allowed. The best is 1110: data 0 + 1 + 4 + 0 = 5, 2 n-links (top-right–bottom-right and bottom-left–bottom-right), cost 5 + 4 = 9. Next: 1010 (12) and 1111 (14). The seed pulls its pixel into the object, and the boundary moves to the right of it.
B5. (a) Each line pixel saves D(0) - D(1) = 4 - 1 = 3; 6 pixels save 18. As object, the line cuts 6 n-links on each side, 12 in total (top and bottom are the image border): cost 12\lambda. Dropped when 12\lambda > 18, i.e. \lambda > 1.5. (b) The band: 18 pixels save 54; it cuts only the 6 n-links on its left side: dropped when 6\lambda > 54, i.e. \lambda > 9. Same intensity, 6 times more robust. (c) Per unit length, a strip of width k gains kg and its two sides cost 2\lambda: it is removed for \lambda > kg/2. Thin structures go first.
B6. (a) Horizontal: \ell vertical n-links, cost \ell, i.e. 1 per unit length. A 45° staircase of Euclidean length \ell goes \ell/\sqrt2 steps right and \ell/\sqrt2 down and cuts one n-link per step: \sqrt2\,\ell, i.e. 1.41 per unit length. (b) Horizontal: per unit length, one vertical n-link (\tfrac12) and two diagonal ones (2 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}): \tfrac12 + \tfrac1{\sqrt2} = 1.207. At 45°, per step of length \sqrt2: one horizontal and one vertical n-link (\tfrac12 + \tfrac12) and two diagonals across the boundary (\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}; the diagonals along the boundary are not cut): (1 + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2})/\sqrt2 = 1.207 per unit length. The same. (c) 8-neighbours: the boundary cost no longer depends on direction (at least for these two directions), so the cut has no reason to prefer axis-aligned edges. With 4-neighbours, diagonal boundaries are 41% more expensive and shapes come out blocky.
B7. V(0,1) + V(1,0) = 2\lambda w_{pq} \ge 0 = V(0,0) + V(1,1). A term that rewards disagreement, V(0,1) < 0 (or that charges more for equal labels than for different ones), violates it; for example a term that wants neighbouring pixels to differ, as in a checkerboard pattern.

title: Exercise: graph-cut segmentation
section: Explore: the graph of a small image
text:
Explore: the graph of a small image
The demo draws a small image as its graph. Pixels show their grey level (0–3) and are framed orange (object) or blue (background) according to the minimum cut. Small images (1 × 3, 2 × 2) show the whole graph with every capacity, and the cut edges dashed red. The 6 × 6 images show the t-links as two bars inside each pixel (left: s \to p, right: p \to t; the cut one is solid), and n-links as lines whose width is \lambda w_{pq}. Click a pixel to change its grey level, or choose label (your cut) and click pixels to make your own labelling; the table then compares its energy with the minimum.



P1. Check B1 and B2 in the demo: the 1 × 3 image at \lambda = 1 and \lambda = 2, then \sigma = 1 at \lambda = 2. Do the cut costs and the max flow match your table?
P2. Choose 2 × 2 (\lambda = 2) and label (your cut). Make the labellings of B3(b) one by one and compare their costs with yours.
P3. Choose 6 × 6 blob (\lambda = 1.5). Which pixels does the minimum cut label differently from thresholding (set \lambda = 0 to see thresholding)? Check that E = data + \lambda \cdot \Sigma w in the table.
P4. Choose thin vs thick and raise \lambda. At which \lambda does the line disappear, and at which the band? Compare with B5.
P5. Choose noisy edge (\lambda = 1, \sigma = 1). One noise pixel in the dark half is labelled object. Why does the cut keep it? Set \sigma = \infty: what happens to it, and to the energy?






Solutions





P1. At \lambda = 1, \sigma = \infty: labelling 101 with cost 3 (data 1, \Sigma w = 2), max flow 3. At \lambda = 2: 111, cost 4. With \sigma = 1 at \lambda = 2: the n-links around the middle pixel shrink to 0.27 each (\lambda w = 2 \cdot 0.135), and 101 is the minimum again with cost 1.54 (shown as data 1, \Sigma w 0.27, \lambda \Sigma w 0.54).
P2. 1100: 6 (the minimum, the demo’s own cut), 1000 and 1110: 9, 1111 and 0000: 14. Every cut you make has cost = energy, and none is below 6.
P3. Thresholding (\lambda = 0) labels 13 pixels object with energy 5: it leaves the dark pixel (grey level 1) inside the blob as background and takes the two isolated pixels of grey level 2 (right of the blob and at the right edge) as object. At \lambda = 1.5 the minimum cut fills the hole and drops both isolated pixels: 12 object pixels, the block of 4 rows and 3 columns. The table shows data 14, \Sigma w 14, E = 14 + 1.5 \cdot 14 = 35 = max flow.
P4. The line disappears at \lambda = 1.5 (at exactly 1.5 the two labellings tie, and the solver drops the line), the band at \lambda = 9 (again a tie). As computed in B5: the band has 9 times the data gain per row but only half the boundary.
P5. The pixel (row 4, column 2, grey level 2) has dark neighbours (0), so with \sigma = 1 each of its 4 n-links has weight e^{-2} = 0.135: isolating it costs only 4 \cdot 0.135 = 0.54, less than the data it saves (4 - 1 = 3). The contrast weights protect it as if it were a real edge. With \sigma = \infty all weights are 1, isolating it costs 4, and the cut drops it; the energy rises from 12.5 to 23, because every boundary is now expensive, including the real one between the halves.

title: Exercise: graph-cut segmentation
text:
Explore: interactive segmentation
A 128 \times 128 image: a synthetic test image (a bright disk with a thin arm, with noise) or a micrograph of a cell. Paint seeds with the mouse: object (red) or background (blue); erase and clear remove them. The intensity model is estimated from the seeds: a Gaussian per label, or a histogram. The large image shows the graph-cut result (orange, with a yellow boundary), the small one thresholding with the same model (\lambda = 0). The table gives the energy of both, the number of object pixels, and, for the test image, the number of wrong pixels compared with the truth. 4 / 8 chooses the neighbourhood; \sigma the contrast weights (\infty: none).



G1. Preset noise (\lambda = 1.5). Compare thresholding and graph cut: wrong pixels, data term and total energy. Which has the smaller data term? Check that the max flow equals E.
G2. Still on noise, move \lambda. Which \lambda gives the fewest wrong pixels? At which \lambda does part of the thin arm disappear, and when is it almost completely gone? Explain with B5.
G3. Preset thin arm lost (\lambda = 6). Now set \sigma = 50. What happens to the arm and to the number of wrong pixels? Why?
G4. Preset blocky (4 neighbours). Describe the shape of the disk. Switch to 8 neighbours. What changes, and what happens to the number of wrong pixels?
G5. Preset nucleus (micrograph, histograms, \lambda = 10, \sigma = 25). Where does the segmentation leak outside the nucleus? Paint a background seed there and see the result update. Then set \sigma = \infty: how does the boundary change?
G6. Preset overlapping intensities: the same object seeds, background seeds only on the white areas. What is segmented, and why? Fix it with a few background strokes on the grey cytoplasm around the nucleus.






Solutions





G1. Thresholding: 2587 wrong pixels, graph cut: 55. The data term of thresholding is smaller (69111.6 against 71491.9): by definition it is the smallest possible data term. But its boundary is enormous (\Sigma w = 7351.0 against 335.6), so its total energy at \lambda = 1.5 is 80138.2, against 71995.3 for the cut. The max flow is 71995.3 = E. (The large numbers come from the constant \log s in the Gaussian data term, the same for every labelling.)
G2. The fewest wrong pixels are at \lambda = 1.5 (55); from \lambda \approx 1 to 1.6 it stays between about 55 and 110. At \lambda = 1.7 the outer half of the arm disappears (wrong pixels jump to 102), at \lambda = 2.75 most of it (137), and from \lambda = 4.7 only a stub of a few pixels is left. The arm is 3 pixels wide: as in B5, its data gain per unit length is about 3g while its two long sides cost 2\lambda (times the 8-neighbour weight 1.21), so it goes long before the disk is affected.
G3. With \sigma = 50 the arm comes back (almost all of it), but the number of wrong pixels rises from 138 to 247. The n-links across the arm’s edges now have small weights (the jump from 80 to 170 is large compared with \sigma), so cutting along the arm is cheap. But noise also produces large differences between neighbours, so noisy pixels are cheaper to cut out as well: more specks survive. Contrast weights help only when edges are larger than the noise.
G4. With 4 neighbours (noise 90, \lambda = 6) the disk comes out as a rounded square with flat horizontal and vertical sides: 457 wrong pixels. With 8 neighbours it is round again and the error falls to 217. With 4 neighbours a diagonal boundary costs 41% more per unit length (B6), so the cut trades the diagonal parts of the circle for axis-aligned ones.
G5. With these seeds the nucleus is found along its envelope (3152 object pixels), with a leak into dark material at the right edge of the image. A background stroke there removes it. With \sigma = \infty (no contrast weights) the boundary no longer follows the dark nuclear envelope: at \lambda = 10 it takes short cuts and the object shrinks to 1779 pixels. The contrast weights make the envelope the cheapest place for the boundary.
G6. The whole cell and its neighbours are segmented (6239 object pixels): the cytoplasm and the other dark material are included. The background model has only seen white, so every grey pixel looks more like the object than like the background; nucleus and cytoplasm have overlapping grey levels, and the data term cannot tell them apart. A few background strokes on the cytoplasm add its grey levels to the background model; with the contrast weights at the envelope the result approaches the nucleus preset.

title: Exercise: graph-cut segmentation
text:
Where this leads
Graph cuts need seeds or a given intensity model, and they find the exact best labelling of a restricted energy. The next unit drops the seeds: normalized cuts look for a balanced split of the whole graph, using an eigenvector of the graph Laplacian.

title: How graphics cards store colour
text:
About this lecture

An image in memory is one long row of bytes. Where is pixel (x, y), channel c?
Layouts: interleaved or planar, channel order, row padding, byte order.
A graphics card (GPU) stores images as textures in a choice of formats: normalised integers, plain integers, floats, packed bits, sRGB. What does each keep, and what does it cost?
The GPU also interpolates (filters) between pixels in hardware. Which formats allow it, and why the stored numbers must be “linear” for it to be right.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

An elective unit, part of the 3D group (taught with the 3D graphics day), after the bit-depth day: that day was about how many bits a value needs and how floats behave. This one is about how values are laid out and encoded, using the GPU as the example because it makes the choices explicit: every texture has a declared format. The concepts (layout, stride, normalised vs float, filtering) apply to any image file or array. No graphics programming is needed or taught.

title: How graphics cards store colour
section: An image is a row of bytes
text:
An image is a row of bytes
A 4 × 2 RGB image, 8 bits per channel:







layout
bytes in memory




interleaved (RGBRGB…)
R G B R G B R G B R G B · R G B … (row 0, then row 1)


planar (RRR…GGG…BBB…)
all R of the image, then all G, then all B




Interleaved keeps one pixel’s channels together: what screens, cameras and textures use.
Planar keeps one channel together: convenient when each channel is processed alone (e.g. a microscope with one image per fluorescent dye).
Channel order is a convention: RGBA or BGRA (common in camera drivers and on Windows). Swap it by mistake and red and blue trade places.

title: How graphics cards store colour
text:
Rows are padded: the stride
Hardware likes rows that start at a multiple of 4 (or more) bytes. Each row may end with unused padding bytes.

Stride (pitch) = bytes from the start of one row to the start of the next, including padding.
An RGB image 1001 pixels wide: 3 \cdot 1001 = 3003 bytes of data per row, padded to a stride of 3004.
Read it with the wrong stride (3003) and row y is read starting y bytes too early: the image is sheared by a third of a pixel per row, and the colours cycle from row to row (each byte is read as the wrong channel).

Always ask an image buffer for its stride; do not compute it from the width.

title: How graphics cards store colour
section: Bytes in a multi-byte number: endianness
text:
Bytes in a multi-byte number: endianness
A 16-bit value occupies two bytes. Which comes first?

Little-endian (almost all CPUs and GPUs today): low byte first. 1000 = 0x03E8 is stored as E8 03.
Big-endian (some file formats, network order): high byte first, 03 E8.
Read little-endian data as big-endian and 1000 becomes 0xE803 = 59 395: a smooth image turns into noise-like garbage, because the low byte changes fastest.

Image file formats state their byte order in the header; 8-bit images do not have the problem.

title: How graphics cards store colour
section: The math: where is a pixel?
text:
The math: where is a pixel?
For an image of width w, height h, C channels of B bytes each, and row stride s \ge w C B, the byte offset of pixel (x, y), channel c is
\text{interleaved: } \; y\,s + x\,C B + c\,B, \qquad \text{planar: } \; c\,(h\,s_1) + y\,s_1 + x\,B,
where s_1 \ge w B is the stride of one plane. The total size is h\,s (interleaved) or C\,h\,s_1 (planar). The matrix index (i, j) of earlier units is (row y, column x); memory is “row-major”: a row is contiguous.

title: How graphics cards store colour
section: Texture formats: what a stored number means
text:
Texture formats: what a stored number means
A GPU texture has a declared format. Three families:









family
stored
the shader reads
example




normalised
integer k, b bits
k/(2^b - 1), a number in [0, 1]
8 bit per channel (RGBA8)


integer
integer k
k itself
16-bit unsigned integer


float
IEEE float
the float
half float (16 bit), float32




Normalised formats make “8 bits” and “10 bits” look the same to the program: both give [0, 1], only the step differs.
Integer formats are exact (labels, raw camera counts), but the hardware cannot interpolate them.
Float formats keep values outside [0, 1], and precision relative to the value (floating-point unit).

title: How graphics cards store colour
text:
Packed formats: bits shared out
When memory or bandwidth is tight, channels get unequal numbers of bits in one 16- or 32-bit word:

5-6-5: red 5 bits, green 6, blue 5 = 16 bits per pixel. Green gets the extra bit because the eye is most sensitive to green (colour day). A grey ramp gets tinted steps, because green steps at different places than red and blue.
10-10-10-2: 10 bits per colour, 2 bits of alpha = 32 bits, the same memory as 8 bits per channel, but 4 times finer steps. Used for HDR displays and medical monitors.

title: How graphics cards store colour
section: Try it: the same data in different formats
text:
Try it: the same data in different formats




The same ramp of values 0.20–0.24 is uploaded twice; the shader stretches 0.20–0.24 to black–white so every stored step shows. 8 bit: 11 bands. 10 bit: 42 bands, much smoother. “565 tint”: coloured bands, because red/blue and green step at different values. “darks: sRGB” on the very dark ramp: linear 8 bit only has codes 0 and 1, sRGB 8 bit has 17 codes there. “half vs float” on the very dark ramp: both smooth. “filter an int”: the integer texture with linear filtering is black. Click a texel to show the stored bits.

title: How graphics cards store colour
section: sRGB storage: more codes for the dark
text:
sRGB storage: more codes for the dark
Light intensities and perceived brightness are not proportional: we notice small differences in dark tones much more than in bright ones.

An sRGB-encoded 8-bit value is not proportional to light: the 256 codes are spaced closely in the dark and widely in the bright. Most 8-bit photos and screenshots are stored this way.
A linear value of 0.005 is code 1 in plain 8 bit, but code 16 in sRGB 8 bit.
An sRGB texture format tells the GPU so: it decodes to linear values when the shader reads the texture, before filtering or blending.
Why the curve has its shape, and why averaging must happen on linear values, is the subject of the colour day. Here: sRGB is a storage encoding, and the GPU undoes it for you if you declare it.

title: How graphics cards store colour
text:
Filtering in hardware
When a texture is drawn larger or smaller than its pixels, the GPU interpolates for free:

nearest: take the closest texel (blocky); linear: bilinear interpolation of the 4 nearest texels (as in the images unit).
Normalised and float formats can be filtered. Integer formats cannot: a texture with linear filtering and an integer format is “incomplete” and reads as black. (Interpolating label 3 and label 7 to give 5 would be wrong anyway.)
Some GPUs cannot filter 32-bit float textures; half floats always can.
Filtering is a weighted average, so it is only right on values proportional to light: hence the sRGB decode first, and premultiplied alpha.

title: How graphics cards store colour
text:
Premultiplied alpha
Alpha \alpha is opacity: 1 = opaque, 0 = fully transparent. A transparent pixel’s colour is meaningless but still stored.

Straight alpha stores (R, G, B, \alpha). Average an opaque red texel with a transparent green one: (0.5, 0.5, 0, 0.5): a half-transparent olive. Green leaks in from a pixel you cannot see: dark or coloured fringes around cut-out objects.
Premultiplied alpha stores (\alpha R, \alpha G, \alpha B, \alpha). The transparent green becomes (0, 0, 0, 0), and the average is (0.5, 0, 0, 0.5): half-transparent red, correct.
So filtering, blending and resizing images with transparency should work on premultiplied values.

title: How graphics cards store colour
section: The math: compositing and filtering with alpha
text:
The math: compositing and filtering with alpha
Drawing a source over a destination (“over” operator, Porter–Duff), with premultiplied colours \mathbf c = \alpha\,\mathbf C:
\mathbf c_\text{out} = \mathbf c_\text{src} + (1 - \alpha_\text{src})\,\mathbf c_\text{dst}, \qquad \alpha_\text{out} = \alpha_\text{src} + (1 - \alpha_\text{src})\,\alpha_\text{dst}.
Both lines have the same form, so premultiplied values are filtered and blended with the same linear formula in every channel. A filter with weights w_i gives \sum w_i \alpha_i \mathbf C_i and \sum w_i \alpha_i; dividing, the true colour is the opacity-weighted average \sum w_i \alpha_i \mathbf C_i / \sum w_i \alpha_i, in which transparent texels have no say. Straight alpha would weight every \mathbf C_i equally.

title: How graphics cards store colour
text:
Mipmaps and memory

A mipmap stores the texture at full, half, quarter, … size, down to 1 × 1. When the texture is drawn small, the GPU reads a pre-shrunk (pre-blurred) level instead of skipping pixels, which would alias (Fourier unit). Cost: +1/3 memory.
Memory = width × height × bytes per texel:

Compressed texture formats store 4 × 4 blocks in 4–8 bits per pixel, lossy, decoded in hardware.

title: How graphics cards store colour
section: The math: why mipmaps cost a third
text:
The math: why mipmaps cost a third
Each level has a quarter of the texels of the one before:
1 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac1{16} + \dots < \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 4^{-k} = \frac{1}{1 - 1/4} = \frac43.
For a 2^n \times 2^n texture the chain has n + 1 levels and \sum_{k=0}^{n} 4^{k} = (4^{n+1} - 1)/3 texels, just under \tfrac43 \cdot 4^n.

title: How graphics cards store colour
text:
Summary

An image in memory: interleaved or planar, a channel order, a stride per row (with padding), and a byte order for multi-byte values. Get one wrong and the image is sheared, recoloured or scrambled.
Texture formats: normalised (k/(2^b - 1)), integer (exact, not filterable), float, packed (5-6-5, 10-10-10-2), sRGB (decoded by the GPU).
Hardware filtering is a weighted average: it needs linear, premultiplied values.
Memory = texels × bytes per texel (× 4/3 with mipmaps).

title: Quiz: images in frequency space
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Why does the discrete Fourier transform lose no information about an image?






Answer





It is a change of basis. An image of N pixels becomes N wave amounts: the same vector written in another coordinate system, as when you describe a point by different axes. Nothing is thrown away, and you can always go back exactly. (In formulas: X = Fx with an invertible matrix F, F^{-1} = \tfrac1N F^* because the waves are orthogonal, and x = F^{-1}X recovers the image.)




Q2. In the centred spectrum of a micrograph, where do you find the information about (a) the overall brightness, (b) the broad shape of the cell, (c) the fine texture and the noise?






Answer






The single centre coefficient, frequency (0, 0): it is N^2 times the mean grey level. (b) Close to the centre: low frequencies. (c) Far from the centre: high frequencies. Note that sharp real edges are high-frequency as well, so a low-pass filter that removes noise also blurs edges.





Q3. An image has a regular pattern of horizontal stripes (lines running left–right), 8 pixels apart, in a 256 × 256 image. Where are the bright dots in its spectrum?






Hint





The brightness changes when you move up and down, not left–right. How many cycles fit in the image?









Answer





On the vertical axis through the centre, at 256/8 = 32 cycles: the pair (u, v) = (0, \pm 32). The dots are perpendicular to the stripes, and come in a mirror pair because the image is real.




Q4. You blur an image by convolving with a 31 \times 31 Gaussian kernel. How else could you compute the same result, and why might it be faster?






Answer





By the convolution theorem: FFT the image and the (zero-padded) kernel, multiply the spectra, inverse FFT. Direct convolution costs about 31^2 \approx 960 multiplications per pixel; the FFT route costs \mathcal{O}(\log N) per pixel. (The Gaussian is also separable: a 31-tap pass along rows then along columns, 62 multiplications per pixel.) Beware: the FFT treats the image as periodic, so pad the image to avoid wrap-around at the border.




Q5. You reduce a photo of a brick wall to a quarter of its size by keeping every 4th pixel in each direction. A strange wavy pattern appears that is not on the wall. What happened, and how do you prevent it?






Answer





Aliasing. The new grid can only hold frequencies up to a quarter of the original Nyquist frequency; the fine brick pattern is above that and folds back as a false, coarser pattern (moiré). Low-pass filter (blur) the image first, so that what the coarse grid cannot represent is removed before sampling.




Q6. A detector adds a faint regular stripe to every image. Should you remove it with a low-pass filter or a notch filter? Why?






Answer





A notch. The stripe is a single wave, so in the spectrum it is one isolated pair of dots; zeroing just those (and their immediate neighbours) removes the stripe and leaves everything else. A low-pass filter would also remove every real structure finer than the stripe.




Q7. A cell sits in the left half of an image. In a second image, the same cell has moved 30 pixels to the right (on the same flat background). How do the two magnitude spectra |X_{u,v}| compare? What has changed in the full spectrum?






Hint





Shifting a wave slides its peaks along. Does it make the wave stronger or weaker?









Answer





The magnitude spectra are the same. Moving the image shifts every wave in it, which changes where its peaks are (its phase), not how strong it is. The magnitude spectrum describes what structures are present, not where; the position is stored in the phases. (Strictly this holds exactly for a shift that wraps around the image, which on a flat background is the same thing.)

title: Exercise: images in frequency space
text:

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the interactive parts. Questions marked (math) ask for derivations; do the others first.

title: Exercise: images in frequency space
text:
By hand
B1. The 8 samples x = (1, 0, -1, 0, 1, 0, -1, 0) are one wave. How many cycles does it complete in the window? Its spectrum has exactly two non-zero coefficients. At which frequencies, and why two?
B2. Predict where the bright dots are in the centred spectrum of a 256 × 256 image of (a) vertical stripes (lines running up and down), 16 pixels apart; (b) horizontal stripes, 4 pixels apart; (c) the sum of the two images. Which dots lie further from the centre, and why?
B3. (Frequency response by numbers.) Filter three signals of length 8 with the blur \tfrac14\,(1, 2, 1) and with the second difference (1, -2, 1), wrapping around at the ends: the flat signal 1, 1, 1, \dots; the slow wave 1, 0, -1, 0, 1, 0, -1, 0; the fastest wave 1, -1, 1, -1, \dots. Each output is the input wave multiplied by a number: find it. Which filter is low-pass and which high-pass? Compare the number for the flat signal with the sum of the weights.
B4. (Shift.) Shift the wave x = (1, 0, -1, 0) one step to the right, wrapping around: y = (0, 1, 0, -1). Its DFT is X = (0, 2, 0, 2), and that of y is Y = (0, -2i, 0, 2i). Compare the sizes |X_k| and |Y_k|. What does a shift change, and what does it keep? What does this mean for the magnitude spectrum of a cell that moves within an image?
B5. (Aliasing.) A stripe pattern repeats every 3 pixels: \cos(2\pi n/3) for n = 0, 1, 2, \dots You halve the image by keeping every 2nd pixel. Write down the kept samples for n = 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. What period do you see in the small image, and what period does that correspond to in the original pixels? Could the small image have shown the true pattern at all? What should you have done before keeping every 2nd pixel?






Solutions





B1. One cycle every 4 samples, so 2 cycles in the window of 8: frequency 2. A real wave such as \cos is the sum of two complex waves, frequency +2 and frequency -2, so it has two coefficients: X_2 = X_6 = 4 (index 6 = 8 - 2 is frequency -2), all others 0. That is the mirror pair.
B2. (a) Vertical stripes change brightness from left to right: dots on the horizontal axis, at 256/16 = 16 cycles, (u, v) = (\pm 16, 0). (b) Horizontal stripes change from top to bottom: dots on the vertical axis at 256/4 = 64, (0, \pm 64). (c) The DFT is linear, so the spectrum of the sum is the sum of the spectra: all four dots. The dots of (b) are four times further out, because those stripes are four times finer (higher frequency). In every case the pair of dots lies perpendicular to the stripes and mirrored through the centre.
B3. Blur, each output is \tfrac14(\text{left} + 2\cdot\text{centre} + \text{right}). Flat: 1, 1, 1, \dots, multiplied by 1. Slow wave: 0.5, 0, -0.5, 0, \dots, multiplied by 0.5. Fastest: \tfrac14(-1 + 2 - 1) = 0 everywhere, multiplied by 0. Second difference, \text{left} - 2\cdot\text{centre} + \text{right}: flat: 0, multiplied by 0. Slow wave: -2, 0, 2, 0, \dots, multiplied by −2. Fastest: -1 - 2 - 1 = -4 at a +1, so -4, 4, -4, \dots, multiplied by −4. The blur keeps the flat signal, halves the slow wave and removes the fastest: low-pass. The second difference removes the flat signal and grows with the frequency (0, 2, 4 in size): high-pass. The number for the flat signal is the sum of the weights: \tfrac14(1 + 2 + 1) = 1 and 1 - 2 + 1 = 0.
B4. |X| = (0, 2, 0, 2) and |Y| = (0, 2, 0, 2): the sizes are the same. The shift changed the complex numbers (2 \to -2i and 2 \to 2i), that is the phase of each wave: it now peaks one step later. The magnitude spectrum is unchanged. So a cell that moves within the image has the same magnitude spectrum: the magnitudes say what structures are there, the phases say where.
B5. The kept samples are \cos(2\pi n/3) at n = 0, 2, 4, \dots: 1, -0.5, -0.5, 1, -0.5, -0.5, 1. They repeat every 3 samples of the small image, which is 6 original pixels: a false pattern twice as coarse as the real one. The small image has pixels 2 original pixels apart and needs at least two samples per cycle, so it can only show periods of 4 original pixels or more: a period of 3 cannot be represented, and it folds back as period 6. Blur (low-pass) the image first, to remove the pattern before keeping every 2nd pixel; then the small image shows a flat grey instead of a false pattern.




Math questions
B6. (math) (Orthogonality.) Show that for integers m, n \ge 1, \int_0^1 \sin(2\pi m t)\,\sin(2\pi n t)\,dt = \begin{cases} 0 & m \ne n,\\ \tfrac12 & m = n.\end{cases} (Use \sin a \sin b = \tfrac12[\cos(a - b) - \cos(a + b)].) If f(t) = \sum_n a_n \sin(2\pi n t), how do you get a_3 back from f?
B7. (math) Compute the DFT X_k = \sum_{n=0}^{3} x_n e^{-2\pi i kn/4} of x = (1, 0, -1, 0) for k = 0, 1, 2, 3. Which wave is x? Why are there two non-zero coefficients for a single wave? (Check your answer against B4.)
B8. (math) Show that for a real signal x, X_{N-k} = \overline{X_k}. Use this to explain why a single stripe pattern in an image gives a pair of dots in its 2D spectrum, mirrored through the centre.
B9. (math) (Shift theorem.) Let y_n = x_{n-m} (indices modulo N: the signal is shifted by m and wraps around). Show that Y_k = e^{-2\pi i km/N}\, X_k. What happens to |X_k|, and what to the phase? What does this mean for the magnitude spectrum of a cell that moves within the image? (Compare with B4.)
B10. (math) (Frequency response.) Filtering with the 1D kernel w = (w_{-1}, w_0, w_1) multiplies the wave e^{i\omega n} by \hat w(\omega) = w_{-1}e^{-i\omega} + w_0 + w_1 e^{i\omega}. Compute \hat w(\omega) for
(a) the blur \tfrac14(1, 2, 1) and (b) the second difference (1, -2, 1).
Evaluate both at \omega = 0 (a constant signal) and \omega = \pi (the fastest wave the grid can hold: +1, -1, +1, \dots). Which is low-pass, which high-pass? Relate \hat w(0) to the sum of the weights. Check your formulas against the numbers of B3, where the slow wave has \omega = \pi/2.






Solutions (math)





B6. \sin(2\pi m t)\sin(2\pi n t) = \tfrac12[\cos 2\pi(m-n)t - \cos 2\pi(m+n)t]. Over one period, \int_0^1 \cos(2\pi j t)\,dt = 0 for any integer j \neq 0 and = 1 for j = 0. If m \ne n both terms integrate to 0. If m = n, the first term is \tfrac12 \cdot 1 and the second 0, giving \tfrac12. So, multiplying f by \sin(2\pi \cdot 3 t) and integrating kills every term except n = 3: a_3 = 2\int_0^1 f(t)\sin(6\pi t)\,dt. This is a projection onto one basis vector.
B7. e^{-2\pi i k n/4} = (-i)^{kn}, and only n = 0 and n = 2 contribute: X_k = 1 - (-i)^{2k} = 1 - (-1)^k. So X = (0, 2, 0, 2). The signal x_n = \cos(2\pi n/4) is one cycle of a cosine. Since \cos\theta = \tfrac12(e^{i\theta} + e^{-i\theta}), it is made of frequency +1 and frequency -1, and index k = 3 = N - 1 is frequency -1.
B8. X_{N-k} = \sum_n x_n e^{-2\pi i (N-k)n/N} = \sum_n x_n e^{-2\pi i n}\, e^{2\pi i kn/N} = \sum_n x_n e^{2\pi i kn/N}, since e^{-2\pi i n} = 1. For real x_n this is the complex conjugate of X_k. A real stripe pattern is a cosine wave, which needs both e^{+i\theta} and e^{-i\theta}: frequencies (u, v) and (-u, -v), a pair of dots mirrored through the centre, with equal magnitude.
B9. Y_k = \sum_n x_{n-m} e^{-2\pi i kn/N}. Substitute p = n - m (the sum runs over all residues modulo N either way): Y_k = \sum_p x_p e^{-2\pi i k(p+m)/N} = e^{-2\pi i km/N} X_k. The factor has modulus 1, so |Y_k| = |X_k|: the magnitude is unchanged and only the phase changes, by -2\pi km/N. The magnitude spectrum of an image does not depend on where the cell is: it describes what structures are present, not where. (This is why the magnitude spectrum is useful as a texture feature, and also why the phase cannot be thrown away when rebuilding an image.)
B10. (a) \hat w(\omega) = \tfrac14(e^{-i\omega} + 2 + e^{i\omega}) = \tfrac14(2 + 2\cos\omega) = \tfrac12(1 + \cos\omega). \hat w(0) = 1: constants pass unchanged. \hat w(\pi) = 0: the fastest wave is removed completely. Low-pass. (b) \hat w(\omega) = e^{-i\omega} - 2 + e^{i\omega} = 2\cos\omega - 2 = -4\sin^2(\omega/2). \hat w(0) = 0: constants are removed. \hat w(\pi) = -4: the fastest wave is amplified 4 times (and flipped). High-pass; for small \omega, \hat w \approx -\omega^2, the frequency response of a second derivative (\tfrac{d^2}{dt^2}e^{i\omega t} = -\omega^2 e^{i\omega t}). In both cases \hat w(0) = \sum w, the sum of the weights.

title: Exercise: images in frequency space
text:
Explore: build a wave
The demo below adds up five waves, a_f \sin(2\pi f\,t) for f = 1, \dots, 5 cycles per window, over one window 0 \le t \le 1. Each slider sets one amplitude a_f and has the same colour as its thin line in the plot; the bold black line is the sum. (A sine is a cosine with phase \varphi = -\pi/2.) The bar chart shows the amplitude spectrum |a_f|: the amount of each frequency, which is what the Fourier transform of the black curve gives back.



W1. Choose pure tone. How many cycles does the sum complete in the window, and what does the spectrum look like? Now set that slider to −1. What changes in the plot, and what changes in the spectrum? Which of the three sinusoid parameters (frequency, amplitude, phase) did the sign change?
W2. Start from all zero, set a_1 = 1, then add a_3 \approx 0.33 and finally a_5 = 0.2 (or press square). Describe how the shape of the sum changes at each step. Roughly what height do the flat parts reach? Which frequencies would you have to add to make the edges steeper still?
W3. Press sawtooth and compare its spectrum with the one for square. Then change the signs of a_2 and a_4 to +1/2 and +1/4. What happens to the signal, and to the spectrum? (Compare with B4 and B9.) Finally, change only a_3 to -1/3. Does the signal still have the same shape? What information does the amplitude spectrum leave out?






Solutions





W1. The pure tone is \sin(2\pi\cdot 2\cdot t): two cycles in the window, and a single bar at f = 2 of height 1. With amplitude −1 the wave is flipped upside down, which is the same as sliding it half a cycle along: the phase changed by \pi. Frequency and the height |a| are the same, so the amplitude spectrum does not change.
W2. a_1 alone is one smooth swell. Adding the third harmonic flattens the tops and steepens the sides; adding the fifth flattens them further, with small ripples on the plateaus. The flat parts sit near \pm\pi/4 \approx \pm 0.79 (that is the limit of \sin x + \tfrac13\sin 3x + \tfrac15\sin 5x + \dots; with three terms the plateaus wiggle around this value). Steeper edges need higher odd harmonics: f = 7, 9, 11, \dots with amplitudes 1/7, 1/9, \dots. Sharp edges live at high frequencies.
W3. The square wave uses only the odd frequencies; the sawtooth uses all five, with heights 1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5. Flipping the signs of a_2 and a_4 gives the same sawtooth, moved by half a window: shifting t by 1/2 multiplies \sin(2\pi f t) by (-1)^f, so it flips exactly the even frequencies. The spectrum is unchanged, as in B4 and B9: a time shift changes the phases, not the amplitudes. Flipping only a_3 is not a shift: the signal gets a clearly different shape, yet the bars are still the same. The amplitude spectrum leaves out the phase of each wave (here only its sign), so different signals can share the same amplitude spectrum. The full Fourier transform keeps the phase too, which is why the signal can be rebuilt from it.

title: Exercise: images in frequency space
text:
Explore: filter an image
The demo below is the lecture’s micrograph (a 256 × 256 crop). Left: the image; middle: its 2D spectrum, log of the magnitude, with frequency 0 in the centre; right: the image rebuilt from the coefficients you keep. Removed coefficients are shown dark red. The radial filters keep the coefficients whose distance r from the centre lies between a min radius and a max radius (the two blue circles; ∞ means no upper limit). The buttons are presets: low-pass sets min = 0, high-pass sets max = ∞, band-pass uses both. The box “keep average brightness (centre)” keeps the centre coefficient whatever the min radius is. The readout gives the share of coefficients kept, the share of the image’s variation they carry, and the RMS error of the rebuilt image (pixel values run from 0 to 1).



E1. Choose low-pass (min radius 0) and set the max radius to 5, 30 and 90. For each, note the percentage of coefficients kept and the percentage of the variation kept. What does that tell you about where the image’s content sits in the spectrum?
E2. Choose keep largest at 3%. Then go back to low-pass and find the max radius that also keeps about 3% of the coefficients. Which of the two has the smaller error? Look at where the kept coefficients lie in the spectrum in “keep largest” mode: why are the two results so similar?
E3. Choose high-pass (max radius ∞) with min radius 10. What is left of the cell? Why is the picture grey rather than black, although most of the low frequencies are gone? Untick keep average brightness (centre) to check your answer.
E4. Tick add stripe artefact and choose no filter: note the error. The stripe adds two bright coefficients to the spectrum, marked with yellow rings. Erase them by dragging over them. What happens to the error? Why are there two dots for one stripe? Then try removing the stripe with a low-pass filter instead, at max radius 15. Which approach is better here?
E5. Go back to low-pass with max radius 30, then raise the min radius from 0 to 5, so that only a ring between the two circles is kept. How many coefficients does that remove, and how much of the variation? What disappears from the image, and what is left? Compare with E1.






Solutions





E1. Radius 5 keeps 0.12% of the coefficients but already 53% of the variation; radius 30 keeps 4.3% of the coefficients and 81% of the variation; radius 90 keeps 39% and 96%. A tiny disc of low frequencies carries most of the variation: the broad light and dark regions. The many high-frequency coefficients each carry little; together they make the fine detail (and the grain). This is why a frequency basis compresses natural images well.
E2. Keep largest 3%: 81% of the variation, RMS error 0.100. Low-pass with max radius 25 also keeps 3.0% of the coefficients: 78% of the variation, error 0.109. Keeping the largest coefficients is slightly better, because it picks the coefficients that matter for this image, while the disc is fixed in advance. They are similar because most of the largest coefficients are low frequencies anyway: in “keep largest” mode the kept coefficients crowd around the centre, with a scatter of single ones further out.
E3. Only edges and fine texture remain: the outline of the nucleus, the membranes, the grain inside the cell. Large uniform regions all become the same grey, because their brightness is low-frequency content. The picture stays grey because the centre coefficient (frequency 0, the average brightness of the whole image) is kept by the “keep average brightness” box, even though it lies inside the min radius. Untick the box and the average of the rebuilt image drops from 0.66 to 0: the values vary around 0, the negative half is shown as black (about half the pixels), and the RMS error jumps from 0.18 to 0.69.
E4. With the stripe and no filter the error is 0.106 (the stripe itself). The stripe is a single 2D wave, so it adds a single bright pair of coefficients, about 19 units from the centre (16 across, 10 down, and its mirror image). Erasing them brings the error down to about 0.02; zeroing exactly the two coefficients would give 0.002, the brush also removes a few of the cell’s own coefficients around them. There are two dots because a real-valued wave is the sum of a frequency and its mirror image (+k and -k), the mirror symmetry of B1 and B8. A low-pass filter at max radius 15 also removes the stripe, but it removes the cell’s detail too: the error is 0.127, worse than leaving the stripe in. A notch removes exactly what you want to remove; a low-pass removes everything above a frequency.
E5. Raising the min radius from 0 to 5 removes very few coefficients: the kept share drops from 4.3% to 4.2% (only 68 of the 65 536 coefficients lie inside radius 5, not counting the centre, which is kept). But the variation kept drops from 81% to 29%, and the RMS error rises from 0.10 to 0.19. As in E1, the few lowest frequencies carry about half of the variation: they are the broad shading, such as the dark nucleus against the lighter cytoplasm. Without them the nucleus becomes the same mid grey as its surroundings, and what is left is structure of intermediate size: the outline of the nucleus, membranes and small organelles, but neither the overall shading (below the min radius) nor the fine grain (above the max radius). A band-pass picks out structures of one size range.

title: Exercise: images in frequency space
text:
Where this leads
Frequency-space features (peaks, orientation, texture energy in a ring) are a classic input for classifying textures. Larger blurs at many scales (a scale space) and the Laplacian of Gaussian come back when we detect objects. The next unit, principal component analysis, is another change of basis: not fixed waves, but directions learned from a set of images.

title: Floating point
text:
About this lecture

Analysis happens in floating point: what is stored, bit by bit, in float32, float16 (half) and bfloat16.
Floats are spaced unevenly: the gap between neighbours grows with the number. What that means for 16-bit images in half floats.
Special values: zero, infinity, NaN, tiny “subnormal” numbers.
Where rounding hurts: cancellation (a negative variance!) and summing millions of pixels.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

The previous unit recommended converting to float before arithmetic. This unit says what that buys and where it still goes wrong. Everything is base-2 scientific notation; the demos let students click bits and see sums drift.

title: Floating point
text:
Scientific notation, in base 2
6.02 \times 10^{23}: a few significant digits and an exponent. Floats do the same in base 2:
x = \pm\, 1.f_1 f_2 \dots f_m \;(\text{binary}) \times 2^{E}.

About 7 significant decimal digits in float32, 3 in float16, 2 in bfloat16.
bfloat16 keeps float32’s exponent range but very few digits (used in machine learning).

title: Floating point
section: Try it: the bits of a float
text:
Try it: the bits of a float




0.1 in float16: 0x2E66, exactly 0.0999755859375. 0.1 has no finite binary expansion, like 1/3 in decimal. Click +1 ulp a few times and watch the value step. Then click the exponent bits: each one doubles or halves. Presets: 2049 becomes 2048 in half; 65535 becomes infinity; switch to float32: 2049 is exact. Smallest subnormal: 6e-8. The plot: the gap between neighbouring floats against the value, a staircase; where it crosses “spacing 1”, integers stop being exact.

title: Floating point
text:
Floats are spaced unevenly
Between two powers of two there are always the same number of floats (2^m), evenly spaced. The next interval is twice as long, so the gaps double:



float16 near
1
1000
3000
65 000




gap to the next float
0.000 98
0.5
2
32




The relative gap is about the same everywhere: 2^{-10} to 2^{-11} for float16. This is machine epsilon, the gap above 1.
Rounding to the nearest float makes a relative error of at most half that: about 0.05 % for float16, 6 \times 10^{-8} for float32.
0.1 is not exactly a float (like 1/3 in decimal). In float16 it is 0.099 975 585 937 5.

title: Floating point
text:
Integers in floats
Every integer is exact as long as the gap is at most 1:



format
all integers exact up to
first one that is not




float32
2^{24} = 16\,777\,216

float16
2^{11} = 2048

A 16-bit image stored in half floats:

values up to 2048 survive; 2049 → 2048, 3001 → 3000, 40 001 → 40 000 (gap 32);
65 535 → infinity: the largest half float is 65 504.
Normalised to [0, 1] instead, the gap near 1 is 2^{-11}: about 11 bits. Half float is fine for 8- or 10-bit data, not for 16-bit.

title: Floating point
text:
Special values

±0: two zeros (the sign is kept, e.g. for 1/(-0) = -\infty).
±∞: overflow (65 535 in half), or 1/0.
NaN (“not a number”): 0/0, \infty - \infty, \sqrt{-1}. Any arithmetic with NaN gives NaN, and NaN ≠ NaN. One NaN pixel spreads through a blur to every pixel it touches; a mean over an image with one NaN is NaN.
Subnormals: below the smallest normal number (2^{-14} \approx 6 \times 10^{-5} in half) the spacing stops shrinking, so the floats run down evenly to 0. Tiny values lose relative precision gradually instead of dropping to 0 at once.

title: Floating point
text:
The math: IEEE 754 numbers
With sign s, stored exponent field E (e bits), fraction field F (m bits) and bias b = 2^{e-1} - 1 (15 for half, 127 for float32):
x = \begin{cases}(-1)^s\, 2^{E - b}\,(1 + F/2^m) & 0 < E < 2^e - 1 \text{ (normal)}\\ (-1)^s\, 2^{1 - b}\,(F/2^m) & E = 0 \text{ (zero, subnormal)}\\ \pm\infty \text{ if } F = 0, \text{ NaN otherwise} & E = 2^e - 1.\end{cases}

In [2^k, 2^{k+1}) the spacing is 2^{k - m}; the relative spacing is between 2^{-m-1} and 2^{-m}; \varepsilon = 2^{-m}.
Round to nearest, ties to even: \operatorname{fl}(x) = x(1 + \delta) with |\delta| \le \varepsilon/2.
Integers are exact while the spacing is \le 1: up to 2^{m+1}.

title: Floating point
text:
Cancellation
Subtracting two nearly equal numbers keeps their absolute error but not their size: the relative error explodes.

In half: 2049 - 2048 gives 0, because 2049 was already stored as 2048.
Textbook variance, \overline{x^2} - \bar x^2: two large, nearly equal numbers. For pixels 10 000, 10 001, 10 002 in float32 it gives 0 (the true value is 2/3): the sum of squares, 300 060 005, is stored as 300 060 000 (gap 32 there).
Fix: compute the mean first, then the squared deviations (two passes), or an update formula that does the same in one pass.

title: Floating point
text:
Summing many pixels
A running sum grows. Once the sum is large, the gap at the sum is larger than the pixel values: each addition rounds, and the small values lose their low bits.

float32: adding 1 to 2^{24} gives 2^{24}. A 2048 × 2048 image with mean 1000 sums to 4 \times 10^9: the naive float32 mean is off by 1 %.
float16: summing normalised pixel values (≈ 0.015 each) gets stuck at 64: from there, adding a pixel rounds back to the same sum.
Pairwise summation (add in a tree: pairs, pairs of pairs, …) keeps partial sums of similar size: error grows like \log n instead of n.
Kahan summation carries the rounding error of each addition into the next one: nearly exact.

title: Floating point
text:
Try it: summing 4 million pixels


Relative error of the sum against the number of pixels. float32 naive is exact up to 2^14 pixels, then drifts to 1 % at 4 million. Pairwise and Kahan stay near 1e-9. float16 naive gets stuck immediately; float16 pairwise is not bad, until “bright and flat”, where the sum of normalised values exceeds 65504 and becomes infinity. Variance: one pass gives a negative number; two passes with naive sums is still off because the mean is off; two passes with pairwise sums is right.

title: Floating point
section: The math: how errors grow when summing
text:
The math: how errors grow when summing
Each addition s_k = \operatorname{fl}(s_{k-1} + x_k) makes a relative error |\delta| \le u = \varepsilon/2. For n non-negative terms (to first order in u):
\text{naive: } |\hat s - s| \lesssim (n - 1)\,u \sum |x_i|, \qquad \text{pairwise: } \lesssim \lceil\log_2 n\rceil\, u \sum |x_i|, \qquad \text{Kahan: } \lesssim 2u \sum |x_i|.
The naive sum stalls when x_k < \tfrac12\operatorname{gap}(s_{k-1}): the addition rounds back to s_{k-1}. Kahan’s trick: after t = \operatorname{fl}(s + y), the quantity c = \operatorname{fl}(\operatorname{fl}(t - s) - y) is exactly the part of y that was lost (with the sign flipped); it is subtracted from the next term.

title: Floating point
text:
Rules of thumb

Do image arithmetic in float32; accumulate long sums (means, histograms of large stacks, integrals) in float64, or pairwise.
Compute variances from deviations from the mean, not from \overline{x^2} - \bar x^2.
Do not test two floats for exact equality; compare with a tolerance relative to their size.
Half floats: fine for display and for values of similar size; not for 16-bit raw data or long sums.
Check for NaN and ∞ after every step that can divide or overflow.

title: Floating point
text:
Summary

A float is \pm 1.f \times 2^E: a fixed number of significant bits, so precision is relative; the gap doubles at every power of two.
float32: 24 significant bits, integers exact to 2^{24}; float16: 11 bits, to 2048, max 65 504; bfloat16: 8 bits.
Special values: ±0, ±∞, NaN (spreads), subnormals.
Subtraction of near-equal values cancels significant bits; long sums drift or stall. Use two-pass variances and pairwise or compensated sums.

title: Camera noise, SNR and PSNR
text:
About this lecture
Where do the numbers in an image come from, and how much of them is noise?

A camera counts electrons: a full well, read noise, an ADC with b bits.
Light itself is noisy: shot noise grows as \sqrt N.
The usual noise model for the rest of the course: additive Gaussian noise of standard deviation \sigma_n, and when it is (and is not) right.
How many bits are worth storing: the dynamic range.
Measuring quality in decibels: SNR and PSNR.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Second unit of the bit-depth day. The quantisation unit showed what rounding to b bits costs; this one asks what the measurement itself can fill. It is the course’s owner of noise models, SNR and PSNR: later days (denoising, MRFs, reconstruction, compression, unmixing) recall the definitions from here. Notation: σ_n is a noise standard deviation; σ alone is reserved for the width of a Gaussian filter.

title: Camera noise, SNR and PSNR
text:
Where the numbers come from
A camera pixel collects light as electrons (e^-), during the exposure:

Full well: a pixel holds at most N_\text{max} electrons (a few thousand to ~100 000). More light: the pixel saturates.
Read noise: the electronics add noise of a few e^- to every reading, even in the dark.
ADC (analogue-to-digital converter): turns the charge into a whole number of ADU (analogue-digital units), with b bits. The gain g says how many electrons one ADU is.

A raw pixel value is “electrons ÷ gain, rounded”.

title: Camera noise, SNR and PSNR
section: Light itself is noisy: shot noise
text:
Light itself is noisy: shot noise
Photons arrive at random. A pixel that collects on average N electrons gets a count that varies from exposure to exposure by about \sqrt N (Poisson statistics):



mean signal N
100
10 000




noise \sqrt N
10
100


signal/noise
10
100




More light → the noise grows, but more slowly than the signal: 100× more light gives 10× better SNR.
The best SNR a pixel can ever reach is \sqrt{N_\text{max}}: for a full well of 30 000 e^-, about 173.
Averaging n frames is like collecting n times the light: the SNR improves by \sqrt n.
So the lowest bits of a bright pixel only record noise.

title: Camera noise, SNR and PSNR
text:
The math: Poisson counts
A count K of independent random arrivals with mean N is Poisson: P(K = k) = e^{-N}N^k/k!, with
\mathbb E[K] = N, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(K) = N, \qquad \text{SNR} = \frac{N}{\sqrt N} = \sqrt N.

The sum of n independent Poisson counts with mean N is Poisson with mean nN: averaging n frames gives mean N and SD \sqrt{N/n}, so the SNR is \sqrt{nN}.
For N \gtrsim 30 the Poisson distribution is close to a Gaussian with mean N and variance N: shot noise behaves like Gaussian noise whose variance equals the signal.

title: Camera noise, SNR and PSNR
text:
The usual noise model
Most methods in this course assume additive Gaussian noise:
\text{observed pixel} = \text{true value} + \text{noise}, \qquad \text{noise} \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma_n^2), \text{ independent from pixel to pixel.}

It fits read noise well, and shot noise in a region of roughly constant brightness (then \sigma_n^2 \approx the mean signal in electrons).
It does not fit across an image with dark and bright parts: shot noise is signal-dependent (bright parts are noisier in absolute terms). At very low light the counts are small whole numbers, not a bell curve.
Saturated pixels have no noise at all, and are not measurements either.
Correlated noise (from demosaicing, compression, or a filter) breaks “independent from pixel to pixel”.


When a method assumes constant σ_n but the noise is Poisson, a variance-stabilising transform (e.g. 2√x, the Anscombe transform) makes the noise roughly constant; mention it as a pointer only. Later days that need a noise model (MRF denoising, wavelet shrinkage, reconstruction, unmixing) recall this slide.

title: Camera noise, SNR and PSNR
section: Try it: how many bits does a camera need?
text:
Try it: how many bits does a camera need?




The plot is a photon-transfer curve: noise against signal, both in electrons, log-log. Flat blue = read noise, slope-1/2 green = shot noise, dashed red = quantisation noise. Start with the sCMOS preset: quantisation is far below everything else. “Same, 8-bit ADC”: now one ADU is 118 electrons, and the dashed line is above the read noise; the dark measured points drop to zero (red triangles), because every pixel of a flat dark patch reads the same number: the signal is lost, not noisy. “Noisy, 16-bit ADC”: the read noise is 66 ADU, so the lowest 6 bits only record noise. Finally the two low-light presets: count the ADU values used in the image (4 with 8 bits, 48 with 12).

title: Camera noise, SNR and PSNR
text:
How many bits are meaningful?

Dynamic range = full well ÷ read noise: the ratio between the brightest signal and the faintest one you can tell from zero. For 30 000 e^- and 1.5 e^-: 20 000 : 1, which is 86 dB, or 14.3 bits.
An ADC with fewer bits than that throws dark detail away (quantisation noise above the read noise).
An ADC with many more bits records noise very precisely: harmless, but the extra bits carry no information.
Rule of thumb: choose the gain so that one ADU is at most about one read-noise SD. Then the read noise works as a natural dither (quantisation unit).
Hence: scientific cameras use 12–16 bits; an 8-bit image of a dim sample may have lost exactly what you wanted to measure.

title: Camera noise, SNR and PSNR
section: The math: adding the noise sources
text:
The math: adding the noise sources
Independent noise sources add in variance. At a mean signal of S electrons, with read noise \sigma_r and gain g:
\sigma^2_\text{total} = \underbrace{S}_{\text{shot}} + \underbrace{\sigma_r^2}_{\text{read}} + \underbrace{g^2/12}_{\text{quantisation}}.

Shot noise dominates when S > \sigma_r^2 (for \sigma_r = 1.5\,e^-: above about 2 electrons).
Quantisation is negligible when g/\sqrt{12} \ll \sigma_r; a full well N_\text{max} spread over 2^b - 1 levels gives g = N_\text{max}/(2^b - 1).
In decibels, amplitude ratios use 20\log_{10}: dynamic range = 20\log_{10}(N_\text{max}/\sigma_r), maximum SNR = 20\log_{10}\sqrt{N_\text{max}} = 10\log_{10}N_\text{max}.
In bits: \log_2(N_\text{max}/\sigma_r); one bit is 20\log_{10}2 \approx 6.02 dB.

title: Camera noise, SNR and PSNR
text:
Measuring noise: SNR and PSNR
SNR (signal-to-noise ratio) of a measurement: the signal divided by the noise SD, \ \text{SNR} = S/\sigma_n. In decibels: 20\log_{10}(S/\sigma_n).

400 electrons with pure shot noise: 400/20 = 20, or 26.0 dB. Halving the noise adds 6 dB.

PSNR (peak signal-to-noise ratio) compares a whole image with a reference (the clean image, or the original before compression or denoising):
\text{MSE} = \text{mean of } (\text{image} - \text{reference})^2, \qquad \text{PSNR} = 10\log_{10}\frac{\text{peak}^2}{\text{MSE}} \text{ dB}.

Peak = the largest possible value: 255 for 8 bits, 2^b - 1 for b bits, 1 for images scaled to [0, 1]. Always state it.
An 8-bit image with Gaussian noise \sigma_n = 5 grey levels: MSE = 25, PSNR = 10\log_{10}(255^2/25) = 34.2 dB. Half the noise: 40.2 dB.
The same 12-bit image (noise 80 ADU) has PSNR 34.2 dB with peak 4095, but 58.3 dB if someone uses the 16-bit peak 65 535: 24 dB for nothing.
PSNR compares pixels one by one; it says nothing about where the errors are or whether they look like structure (the quantisation unit’s dithering example).


PSNR is the standard number for denoising, compression and reconstruction results; SSIM and “metrics can disagree” are left to the compression day. With an image scaled to [0, 1], peak = 1 and PSNR = −10 log10(MSE). In a physical unit (electrons) the natural peak is the full well. The quantisation unit’s SNR (signal variance over rounding-noise variance) is a third variant: say which one you use.

title: Camera noise, SNR and PSNR
section: The math: decibels for SNR and PSNR
text:
The math: decibels for SNR and PSNR
Decibels measure a power (variance) ratio P_1/P_2 as 10\log_{10}(P_1/P_2); for an amplitude (SD) ratio that is 20\log_{10}(A_1/A_2).

Averaging n frames divides the noise variance by n: +10\log_{10}n dB (+6.0 dB for 4 frames, +12.0 dB for 16).
Rounding to b bits on a [0, 2^b - 1] scale (step \Delta = 1) gives MSE = \Delta^2/12, so

\text{PSNR}_\text{quantisation} = 10\log_{10}\frac{(2^b - 1)^2}{1/12} = 20\log_{10}(2^b - 1) + 10\log_{10}12 \approx 6.02\,b + 10.8 \text{ dB}
(58.9 dB for 8 bits). Noise well below that is invisible next to the rounding.

A PSNR difference between two methods on the same image and peak is 10\log_{10}(\text{MSE}_1/\text{MSE}_2): independent of the peak.

title: Camera noise, SNR and PSNR
text:
Summary

A camera counts electrons: shot noise \sqrt N (Poisson), read noise, a full well. Their ratio, the dynamic range, says how many bits are worth storing.
Noise sources add in variance. Averaging n frames improves the SNR by \sqrt n.
The usual model is additive Gaussian noise \sigma_n; shot noise is signal-dependent, so the model holds region by region.
SNR = signal / noise SD; PSNR = 10\log_{10}(\text{peak}^2/\text{MSE}) against a reference, with the peak stated.
Next: storing and showing those 12- and 16-bit numbers without breaking them.

title: Quiz: from PCA to autoencoders
text:
Short questions on encoders, decoders and PCA. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. An encoder maps an image to a few numbers z; a decoder maps z back to an image; an autoencoder trains both so that decode(encode(image)) is close to the image.

Q1. In one sentence each: what does the encoder do, what does the decoder do, and what is an autoencoder trained to achieve?






Hint





Think of the hourglass: wide, narrow, wide.









Answer





The encoder compresses an image into a few numbers z (its place in the latent space). The decoder rebuilds the whole image from z alone. Both are trained together so that the rebuilt image is as close as possible to the input, for many images at once.




Q2. PCA with one component, PC1 = (0.6,\ 0.8), a two-pixel image with the mean subtracted, \mathbf x = (1,\ 2). Encode, decode, and give the squared reconstruction error.






Hint





Encode = dot product with PC1. Decode = score × PC1.









Answer





Score = 0.6 + 1.6 = 2.2. Decoded 2.2 \cdot (0.6,\ 0.8) = (1.32,\ 1.76). Error (-0.32,\ 0.24), squared length 0.1024 + 0.0576 = 0.16.




Q3. Why must the bottleneck be narrow? What would an autoencoder with a 784-number bottleneck learn on 28\times28 images?






Hint





What is the cheapest way to make the output equal the input?









Answer





With a bottleneck as wide as the input it can pass the image straight through (or rotate it and rotate it back, as PCA with all components does). The reconstruction is perfect but z summarises nothing. A narrow bottleneck forces z to keep only the main ways in which the images differ.




Q4. For the same data, which has the smaller reconstruction error with 2 numbers per image: PCA, or a trained autoencoder whose encoder and decoder have no ReLU?






Hint





What is a network without bends?









Answer





They are (at best) equal. Without bends, encoder and decoder are linear maps, and among linear encoder/decoder pairs with 2 numbers PCA already has the smallest squared error. Only the bends let an autoencoder beat PCA.




Q5. Images of a cell that slowly elongates lie on a curve in pixel space. Why can a nonlinear autoencoder describe them with one number, where PCA needs several?






Hint





Straight line or curve?









Answer





PCA decodes along straight lines (flat subspaces), so a curved family needs several directions to hold its bends. A nonlinear decoder maps one number to a curve, which can follow the family: one number says how far along the elongation the cell is.




Q6. In a 28\times28 PCA, what does a principal component look like if you display it?






Hint





How many entries does it have?









Answer





It has 784 entries, so it can be shown as a 28\times28 image (an “eigen-image”), with positive and negative values. Decoding adds the mean image and the eigen-images weighted by the scores.
