B9. (math) Show that after one step w_\text{new} - 1.5 = (1 - 8\eta)(w - 1.5). For which \eta does every step bring w closer to the best value?






Solutions (math)





B9. (math) w_\text{new} = w + 4\eta(3 - 2w) = w + 8\eta(1.5 - w), so w_\text{new} - 1.5 = (w - 1.5) - 8\eta(w - 1.5) = (1 - 8\eta)(w - 1.5). The distance shrinks at every step when |1 - 8\eta| < 1, i.e. 0 < \eta < 0.25. For 0.125 < \eta < 0.25 it zigzags across the valley but still converges.

title: Exercise: neural networks
text:
Explore
The demo fits a small network (1 \to H \to 1) to a line scan across two nuclei of different brightness (synthetic data with noise). Grey dots are the pixels, the red curve is the network, the faint orange curves are the hidden units’ hinges (each times its output weight) and the orange triangles mark where they bend. Below: the loss against the training step. train 500 steps runs gradient descent; new start puts the hinges back at their (fixed-seed) starting positions.



E1. With 3 hidden units, press train 500 steps six times. Where do the three hinges end up? Which features of the profile does the network get, and which does it miss?
E2. Compare the presets one hinge, 3 hinges and 12 hinges: read the final loss of each. The noise in the data has variance 0.03^2 = 0.0009. Which network is close to the best you can hope for? Can a network do better than the noise level on these data, and would that be good?
E3. Preset no bend: 12 hidden units, but no ReLU. Describe the fit and compare its loss with a flat line at the mean intensity (loss 0.0728). Explain with the collapse argument from the lecture.
E4. Preset learning rate too large. What happens to the loss, and to the hinges at the end? What does the fit look like?






Solutions





E1. After 3000 steps the three hinges sit at about 0.04, 0.27 and 0.47 on the 0–1 axis: the left foot, the top and the right foot of the bright nucleus. The network makes a tent over the bright nucleus and a flat line (about 0.33) to the right of it: the dimmer nucleus is missed. Three hinges are not enough for two plateaus with four edges. Loss 0.0203.
E2. Final losses after 3000 steps: one hinge 0.0588, 3 hinges 0.0203, 12 hinges 0.00186. Only the 12-hinge network is close to the noise variance 0.0009. A network with very many units could push the loss below 0.0009 by following the noise from pixel to pixel; that would be overfitting: it would fit these 100 pixels better but a new line scan of the same nuclei worse.
E3. The fit stays a straight, slightly tilted line, loss 0.0652, barely better than the flat line at the mean (0.0728). Without the bend, twelve hidden units and the output layer collapse to one matrix: \text{out} = (CA)x + \text{shift}, a straight line, however many units there are.
E4. The loss jumps around instead of falling smoothly, and after 500 steps it sits at 0.0728, exactly the loss of the flat mean line: every hinge has been thrown off the data (no unit is switched on anywhere between 0 and 1), so the network outputs a constant. The steps were so large that they overshot into a region where the ReLUs are off and the gradient is zero, and the network can no longer recover (“dead units”). A smaller learning rate avoids this.

title: Exercise: neural networks
text:
Where this leads
The rest of the neural-networks day uses the same “matrix, bend, matrix” with whole images as input (a 784-number vector for a 28\times28 image), many layers and many training examples: losses for classification, backpropagation, and convolutional networks that segment images. Later, the autoencoder units squeeze an image through a few numbers and rebuild it; without the bend such a network is exactly PCA.

title: Quiz: neural networks
text:
Short questions on layers, the ReLU bend and training. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. A layer computes \text{ReLU}(A\mathbf x + \mathbf b) with \text{ReLU}(s) = \max(0, s) on each entry; training steps the weights against the gradient of a loss.

Q1. Compute \text{ReLU}\big((2,\ -3,\ 0,\ 0.5)\big).






Hint





Entry by entry: negatives become 0, the rest pass through.









Answer





(2,\ 0,\ 0,\ 0.5).




Q2. A colleague stacks ten layers, each a matrix plus a shift, with no ReLU in between. Can this network fit a curved intensity profile better than a single layer?






Hint





What is C(A\mathbf x + \mathbf b) + \mathbf d?









Answer





No. C(A\mathbf x + \mathbf b) + \mathbf d = (CA)\mathbf x + (C\mathbf b + \mathbf d): one matrix and one shift. However many layers, the result is a straight-line (linear) map. Only the bend between layers allows curves.




Q3. A network with one input x has three ReLU hidden units and one linear output. What does its output look like as a function of x?






Hint





Each hidden unit is \max(0, a_k x + b_k).









Answer





A continuous, piecewise straight line with at most three bends, one where each unit switches on (x = -b_k/a_k). Between the bends it is straight. More units allow more bends.




Q4. You train with gradient descent and the loss jumps up and down and grows. What is the first thing to change?






Hint





What controls the size of each step?









Answer





Lower the learning rate \eta. Steps that are too large overshoot the bottom of the valley and land higher on the other side; if each overshoot is larger than the last, the loss grows.




Q5. How many numbers (weights and shifts) does a layer from a 28\times 28 image to 64 hidden units have?






Hint





The matrix is 64 \times 784; one shift per hidden unit.









Answer





784 \cdot 64 + 64 = 50{,}240.




Q6. Why do neural networks for images need many training images?






Hint





Compare the number of weights with the number of examples.









Answer





They have very many weights (hundreds of thousands). With few images, many different weight settings fit them equally well, including ones that just memorise the training images and fail on new ones. Many examples (or a penalty, or a smaller network) pin the weights down; checking on images not used for training shows whether it worked.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
About this lecture
The Fourier unit rewrote an image in a fixed basis of waves. PCA finds a basis from the data: the directions in which a set of images (or patches, or pixels) actually varies.

Many small images are a cloud of points: one axis per pixel.
Centre the cloud, then find the direction of most spread: the first principal component.
The covariance matrix holds all the spreads; its eigenvectors are the principal components.
Keep a few scores, rebuild the rest: projection and reconstruction, and how many components to keep.
Image examples: two-pixel images, 8×8 patches, colour pixels.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

This is the course’s PCA unit: every later day that needs PCA (the region’s principal axes, shape models, colour decorrelation, compression, unmixing, autoencoders) recalls it from here. Linear algebra needed: dot product, unit vectors, eigenvectors of a symmetric 2 × 2 matrix. The covariance is divided by n throughout (as in the autoencoder unit); with n − 1 the eigenvectors are the same and the eigenvalues scale by n/(n − 1).

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Two pixels, one point




Take two neighbouring pixels of a smooth image: a tiny image with two grey values (p_1, p_2). Draw it as a point, pixel 1 across, pixel 2 up.

150 such pairs make a cloud. The two pixels are almost equally bright, so it lies along the diagonal.
The cloud is long in one direction (overall brightness of the pair) and thin in the other (the small difference, a tiny edge).
One number, the position along the blue line, almost describes each pair. Red: what that one number misses.

A 28 \times 28 image is a point with 784 coordinates. Same idea; we just cannot draw it.


The data are the “neighbouring pixels” preset of the demo (and of the autoencoder unit’s demo): brightness uniform in [0.15, 0.85], difference ±0.06 (normal), fixed seed. Ask the class first: if the pixels were far apart in the image, what would the cloud look like? (Rounder: far-apart pixels are less related.)

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Step 1: centre the cloud
Subtract the mean image \bar{\mathbf x} (the average of each pixel) from every image.

The cloud now sits around the origin. Directions are measured from the centre of the data, not from black (0, 0).
Without centring, the “best direction” through (0, 0) mostly points at the mean: it describes how bright the images are on average, which we already know, instead of how they differ.
Every later step works on the centred images \mathbf x - \bar{\mathbf x}; the mean is added back at the end.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Spread along a direction
Pick a direction: a unit vector \mathbf u (length 1). Each centred image gets one number, its score:
s = \mathbf u \cdot (\mathbf x - \bar{\mathbf x}) \qquad \text{(how far along } \mathbf u \text{ the image lies)}

The scores of all images have a variance: the spread of the cloud along \mathbf u.
Turn \mathbf u: the variance changes. For the neighbouring pixels it is largest along the diagonal, smallest across it.
PC1 (first principal component) = the direction of largest variance. PC2 = the largest among the directions perpendicular to PC1 (in 2D: simply the perpendicular).

title: Principal component analysis
section: Try it: the shape of a point cloud
text:
Try it: the shape of a point cloud




Start at u = 0° (keep pixel 1 only): variance 0.0406, error 0.0414. Drag u round: the blue curve peaks at the orange tick (PC1, 45.3°, variance 0.0762), the red error curve bottoms out there (0.0058 = λ2). Blue + red is always tr S = 0.0820. Then “four images” (the next slides’ example). Then “one outlier”: a single hot pixel turns PC1 and drops PC1’s share from 93 % to 70 %. Then “no centring”: the line through (0, 0) is far worse than PCA. Drag dots to make the cloud round, or long in another direction.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
The covariance matrix, by hand
Four two-pixel images: (0.2, 0.4), (0.4, 0.2), (0.6, 0.8), (0.8, 0.6).

Mean image (0.5, 0.5). Centred: (-0.3, -0.1), (-0.1, -0.3), (0.1, 0.3), (0.3, 0.1).
Average the products, over the 4 images:

S = \begin{pmatrix} \overline{y_1^2} & \overline{y_1 y_2} \\ \overline{y_2 y_1} & \overline{y_2^2} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.05 & 0.03 \\ 0.03 & 0.05 \end{pmatrix}

Diagonal: the variance of each pixel (0.05 each). Off-diagonal: the covariance, positive because the pixels tend to be bright together.
The variance along any unit vector \mathbf u follows from S alone (math slide). Along the diagonal \mathbf u = (1, 1)/\sqrt2: 0.08. Across it, (1, -1)/\sqrt2: 0.02. Along pixel 1, (1, 0): 0.05.


y = x − mean. Products for the off-diagonal: 0.03, 0.03, 0.03, 0.03, average 0.03. This is the demo’s “four images” preset: the readout shows the same S. The total variance (sum of the diagonal) is 0.10; it is the same in every orthogonal pair of directions: 0.05 + 0.05 = 0.08 + 0.02.

title: Principal component analysis
section: The math: the best direction is an eigenvector
text:
The math: the best direction is an eigenvector
Centred images \mathbf y_i = \mathbf x_i - \bar{\mathbf x}, covariance S = \frac1n\sum_i \mathbf y_i\mathbf y_i^\top (symmetric, d \times d). The variance of the scores along a unit vector \mathbf u:
\frac1n\sum_i (\mathbf u^\top\mathbf y_i)^2 = \frac1n\sum_i \mathbf u^\top\mathbf y_i\,\mathbf y_i^\top\mathbf u = \mathbf u^\top S\,\mathbf u.
Maximise \mathbf u^\top S\mathbf u subject to \mathbf u^\top\mathbf u = 1. With a Lagrange multiplier \lambda, setting the gradient of \mathbf u^\top S\mathbf u - \lambda(\mathbf u^\top\mathbf u - 1) to zero:
2S\mathbf u - 2\lambda\mathbf u = 0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad S\mathbf u = \lambda\mathbf u, \qquad \text{and then } \mathbf u^\top S\mathbf u = \lambda.

So the stationary directions are the eigenvectors of S, and the variance along each is its eigenvalue. The largest eigenvalue \lambda_1 gives PC1.
S is symmetric, so (spectral theorem) its eigenvectors can be chosen orthonormal, and all \lambda_k \ge 0. Order them descending: \lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_d.
For S = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix}: eigenvectors (1, \pm1)/\sqrt2, eigenvalues a \pm b. The example: 0.05 \pm 0.03.

title: Principal component analysis
section: Principal components: new axes for the data
text:
Principal components: new axes for the data
The eigenvectors \mathbf u_1, \mathbf u_2, \dots of S, ordered by eigenvalue (largest first), are the principal components.

They are perpendicular to each other: a rotated set of axes, fitted to the cloud.
The eigenvalue \lambda_k is the variance of the scores along \mathbf u_k.
In the new axes the scores are uncorrelated: the cloud’s tilt is gone.
Nothing is lost by rotating: the total variance (sum of the pixel variances) equals \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \dots. In the example 0.05 + 0.05 = 0.08 + 0.02.
Share of PC1: 0.08 / 0.10 = 80\,\%. For the 150 neighbouring pixel pairs: 93\,\%.


In the demo, the ellipse is the 2-SD contour of a Gaussian with covariance S: its axes are the PCs and its half-lengths are 2√λ. Sign: −u is as good as u; programs may return either.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Projection and reconstruction
Keep only the first k scores, s_j = \mathbf u_j \cdot (\mathbf x - \bar{\mathbf x}), and rebuild:
\hat{\mathbf x} = \bar{\mathbf x} + s_1\mathbf u_1 + \dots + s_k\mathbf u_k.
The example, k = 1, image (0.2, 0.4), \mathbf u_1 = (1, 1)/\sqrt2:

Score s_1 = \big((-0.3) + (-0.1)\big)/\sqrt2 = -0.283: the pair is darker than average.
Rebuilt: (0.5, 0.5) + s_1\,\mathbf u_1 = (0.5, 0.5) - (0.2, 0.2) = (0.3, 0.3): same brightness, the difference is gone.
Error (0.2, 0.4) - (0.3, 0.3) = (-0.1, 0.1), squared length 0.02. All four images lose 0.02: the mean error is \lambda_2 = 0.02, the variance that was dropped.

With all components the reconstruction is exact: rotate, rotate back. The saving comes from keeping few.

title: Principal component analysis
section: The math: the error is the sum of the dropped eigenvalues
text:
The math: the error is the sum of the dropped eigenvalues
Write a centred image in the PC basis: \mathbf y = \sum_{j=1}^d s_j\mathbf u_j with s_j = \mathbf u_j^\top\mathbf y. Keeping the first k terms leaves \mathbf y - \hat{\mathbf y} = \sum_{j > k} s_j\mathbf u_j, and since the \mathbf u_j are orthonormal,
\|\mathbf y - \hat{\mathbf y}\|^2 = \sum_{j > k} s_j^2, \qquad \frac1n\sum_i\|\mathbf y_i - \hat{\mathbf y}_i\|^2 = \sum_{j > k}\lambda_j = \operatorname{tr}S - \sum_{j \le k}\lambda_j.

For one direction \mathbf u (not necessarily a PC): mean error = \operatorname{tr}S - \mathbf u^\top S\mathbf u (Pythagoras for each image). Smallest error ⇔ largest variance kept: the same \mathbf u_1.
More generally (Eckart–Young): no k-dimensional flat subspace through the mean fits the images better in squared error than the first k PCs.
The scores are uncorrelated: \frac1n\sum_i s_{ij}s_{il} = \mathbf u_j^\top S\mathbf u_l = \lambda_l\,\mathbf u_j^\top\mathbf u_l = 0 for j \ne l.

title: Principal component analysis
section: How many components? The scree plot
text:
How many components? The scree plot


Plot the eigenvalues, largest first (a scree plot), or the cumulative share of the variance.
Keep components up to the “elbow”, or until a target share is reached (90 %: here 11 of 64 numbers per patch).
The small eigenvalues are often mostly noise: dropping them also denoises.


Numbers computed with NumPy from the course micrograph (cell256.png, values scaled to [0, 1]): all 62 001 overlapping 8 × 8 patches, covariance divided by n. Shares: 68.5, 6.2, 4.3, 2.5, 2.1 % for PC1–5; cumulative 89.3 % at 10 components, 90 % needs 11, 95 % needs 24, 99 % needs 50. Rebuilding the image from non-overlapping patches with 1, 4 and 10 components gives RMS errors 0.131, 0.100 and 0.076. There is no universal rule for k: the elbow, a share, or what the next step (classification, display, compression) needs.

title: Principal component analysis
section: PCA and Fourier: two changes of basis
text:
PCA and Fourier: two changes of basis
Both rewrite an image (or patch) as a weighted sum of basis images, with orthonormal basis vectors: rotate, keep the important coefficients, rotate back.









Fourier (DFT/DCT)
PCA




basis
fixed waves, the same for every image set
learned from the data: eigenvectors of S


order
by frequency
by variance in these data


best for
any image; fast to compute
the data it was fitted on: fewest components for a given error




On the micrograph’s patches, the PCs look like waves: flat, then slow ramps, then faster patterns. PC1–3 match the three lowest cosine waves (overlap 0.97 or more). For images whose statistics are the same everywhere, PCA and cosines nearly agree, which is why JPEG can use the fixed cosines.
On a special data set (faces, cell shapes, one kind of tissue) the learned basis wins.


“Overlap” is |dot product| of the unit-length PC and the best-matching 8 × 8 DCT basis image: 0.999 (PC1, the flat patch), 0.981 (PC2), 0.973 (PC3); PC4 and PC5 are mixtures (0.76). Same NumPy computation as the scree figure. The theorem behind “PCA ≈ Fourier”: for a stationary process the covariance of a patch is (nearly) a convolution matrix, and convolution matrices are diagonalised by the Fourier basis (the convolution theorem of the Fourier unit). PCA under the name Karhunen–Loève transform is the optimal (but data-dependent) transform coder.

title: Principal component analysis
section: Colour pixels: three numbers per pixel
text:
Colour pixels: three numbers per pixel
A colour pixel (R, G, B) is a point in 3D; the pixels of a photograph are a cloud.

In most scenes the three channels rise and fall together (light and shadow change all three). PC1 points close to (1, 1, 1)/\sqrt3: brightness, carrying most of the variance.
PC2 and PC3 are colour differences (e.g. red against blue, green against magenta), with much less variance.
That is why image formats store brightness plus two colour differences, and give the differences fewer bits or fewer pixels: the decorrelation PCA would find, fixed in advance.
For a stained tissue section the PCs follow the stains, not the screen colours: a starting point for separating them.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
When PCA misleads

Outliers: variance is a sum of squares, so one hot pixel or one bad image can turn PC1 (demo: “one outlier”).
Units: mix a cell area in µm² with an intensity in [0, 1], and PC1 is simply “area”. Standardise each feature (divide by its standard deviation) first when units differ.
Nearly equal eigenvalues: a round cloud has no preferred direction; the PCs swing when one point moves. Report the subspace, not the individual axes.
Curved clouds: PCA fits flat subspaces. Images of a moving spot lie on a curve; one PCA score folds it. A nonlinear autoencoder can follow it (the VAE units).
PCA finds directions of variance, not of meaning: the largest spread may be lighting, not biology.

title: Principal component analysis
text:
Summary







Idea
In one line




Image as a point
one axis per pixel; a set of images is a cloud


Centre
subtract the mean image first


Covariance S
pixel variances on the diagonal, covariances off it


Principal components
eigenvectors of S, largest eigenvalue first; perpendicular; scores uncorrelated


Eigenvalue
the variance along that component; they add up to the total variance


Reconstruction
mean + scores × components; error = the dropped eigenvalues


Scree plot
how many components carry most of the variance


vs Fourier
both a change of basis: Fourier fixed, PCA learned from the data

title: Exercise: quantisation and bit depth
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute the number of levels and the step for a given bit depth, and quantise values by hand,
predict where banding appears and explain what dithering changes,
predict how the rounding error and the SNR change with the bit depth (about 6 dB per bit).

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the interactive part. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: quantisation and bit depth
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute the number of levels and the step for a given bit depth, and quantise values by hand,
predict where banding appears and explain what dithering changes,
predict how the rounding error and the SNR change with the bit depth (about 6 dB per bit).

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the interactive part. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: quantisation and bit depth
text:
By hand
B1. How many grey levels do a 10-bit and a 14-bit sensor have? By about what factor is the step of a 12-bit image finer than that of an 8-bit image, if both cover black to white?
B2. Quantise the row of values (as fractions of the full range) 0.10,\quad 0.22,\quad 0.37,\quad 0.55,\quad 0.81 to 2 bits, i.e. to the levels 0, \tfrac13, \tfrac23, 1. Give the codes k \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}, the stored values and the errors. What is the largest error that rounding can ever make here?
B3. A flat region has the value 0.25 everywhere and is quantised to 2 bits. (a) Without dither, what does every pixel become, and what is the error? (b) With random dither, a pixel rounds up to \tfrac13 with some probability and down to 0 otherwise. Predict that probability, and the average over many pixels.
B4. A smooth ramp from black to white is quantised to 6 bits and to 10 bits. Use the rule “about 6 dB per bit” to predict the SNR of the rounding in each case, and give the RMS error \Delta/\sqrt{12} as a fraction of the range. How many times smaller is the 10-bit error?






Solutions





B1. 2^{10} = 1024 and 2^{14} = 16\,384 levels. The steps are 1/255 and 1/4095 of the range: the 12-bit step is 4095/255 \approx 16 times finer.
B2. Multiply by 3 and round: 0.30 \to 0, 0.66 \to 1, 1.11 \to 1, 1.65 \to 2, 2.43 \to 2. Stored values 0, \tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac23, \tfrac23. Errors (stored − true): -0.100, +0.113, -0.037, +0.117, -0.143. Rounding never moves a value by more than half a step, \Delta/2 = \tfrac16 \approx 0.167.
B3. (a) 0.25 \times 3 = 0.75 rounds to 1: every pixel becomes \tfrac13, an error of +0.083 everywhere. The whole region is too bright by the same amount: no average can fix that. (b) The value is 75 % of the way from level 0 to level 1, so a pixel rounds up with probability 0.75: three quarters of the pixels become \tfrac13, one quarter 0. The average is 0.75 \cdot \tfrac13 = 0.25, the true value.
B4. About 6 \cdot 6 = 36 dB and 6 \cdot 10 = 60 dB (exactly 20\log_{10}63 = 36.0 and 20\log_{10}1023 = 60.2 dB). RMS error \frac{1}{63\sqrt{12}} = 0.0046 and \frac{1}{1023\sqrt{12}} = 0.00028 of the range: 1023/63 \approx 16 times smaller, 2^4 for 4 more bits.




Math questions
B5. (math) Let the rounding error e be uniform on [-\Delta/2, \Delta/2]. Show that \operatorname{Var}(e) = \Delta^2/12. A signal spread evenly over the full range R = (2^b - 1)\Delta has variance R^2/12: show that the SNR is 20\log_{10}(2^b - 1) \approx 6.02\,b dB, and evaluate it for b = 4.
B6. (math) Random dither: in units of \Delta, x = k + f with 0 \le f < 1 and u uniform on [-\tfrac12, \tfrac12). Show that \mathbb E[\operatorname{round}(x + u)] = x, and that the mean squared error, averaged over f uniform on [0, 1), is \Delta^2/6. By what factor is the RMS error larger than without dither?






Solutions (math)





B5. \mathbb E[e] = 0 by symmetry, so \operatorname{Var}(e) = \int_{-\Delta/2}^{\Delta/2} e^2 \tfrac{1}{\Delta}\,de = \tfrac{1}{\Delta}\cdot\tfrac{2}{3}\left(\tfrac{\Delta}{2}\right)^3 = \tfrac{\Delta^2}{12}. Then \text{SNR} = 10\log_{10}\frac{R^2/12}{\Delta^2/12} = 20\log_{10}(2^b - 1) \approx 20\,b\log_{10}2 = 6.02\,b dB. For b = 4: 20\log_{10}15 \approx 23.5 dB (6.02 · 4 = 24.1 is the large-b approximation). The demo’s ramp at 4 bits shows exactly 23.5 dB.
B6. x + u reaches the rounding threshold k + \tfrac12 when u \ge \tfrac12 - f, with probability f; then the output is k + 1, otherwise k. So \mathbb E = (1-f)k + f(k+1) = x. The error is 1 - f (probability f) or -f (probability 1-f): \mathbb E[e^2] = f(1-f)^2 + (1-f)f^2 = f(1-f), and \int_0^1 f(1-f)\,df = \tfrac12 - \tfrac13 = \tfrac16. In units of \Delta^2: \Delta^2/6, twice \Delta^2/12, so the RMS error is \sqrt2 \approx 1.41 times larger. (The demo: 0.0272 vs 0.0192 on the ramp at 4 bits, a ratio of 1.42.)

title: Exercise: quantisation and bit depth
text:
Explore

Quantising an image
The demo rounds an image to b bits and shows the rounding error (0 = grey, \pm\Delta = white/black) and its histogram. Images: a ramp, smooth blobs, and the 8-bit micrograph.



E1. On the ramp, step the bits from 8 down to 1. Compare the RMS error with \Delta/\sqrt{12} in the readout. How much does the SNR change per bit?
E2. Click 4 bits: banding, then 4 bits + dither. What happens to the contour lines, to the error histogram, and to the RMS error? Which picture looks closer to the original?
E3. Micrograph at 2 bits: compare no dither and error diffusion. Which has the larger RMS error? Which shows the cell better? What does that tell you about RMS error as a measure of image quality?
E4. Micrograph at 8 bits: the RMS error is 0. Why?






Solutions





E1. They agree to the 4th decimal at every bit depth (e.g. 0.0192 at 4 bits, 0.0046 at 6 bits): on a ramp the error is exactly uniform. The SNR goes 23.5, 29.8, 36.0 dB for 4, 5, 6 bits: about 6 dB per bit.
E2. The contour lines disappear and become fine grain. The histogram changes from a box on \pm\Delta/2 to a triangle on \pm\Delta, and the RMS error grows from 0.0192 to 0.0273, about \sqrt2 times. Yet the dithered image looks closer to the original from a distance: its error has no structure, and the eye averages it away.
E3. Error diffusion has the larger RMS error (0.1200 against 0.0968), but it shows far more of the cell: with only 4 grey levels, the local average of the diffused pixels follows the true grey value. The RMS error compares pixels one by one and ignores what the eye does, which is to average neighbours. A small number is not always a better picture.
E4. The micrograph is stored with 8 bits already, so every value is exactly one of the 256 levels and rounding changes nothing. Quantising can only lose information; it cannot add the bits that were never measured.

title: Exercise: quantisation and bit depth
text:
Where this leads
Rounding is only one source of error in a pixel value. The next unit, camera noise, asks where the numbers come from: a camera counts electrons, the count is noisy, and that noise, not the rounding, usually decides how many bits are worth storing. It also defines the SNR and PSNR used in the rest of the course.

title: Quiz: quantisation and bit depth
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A camera has a 12-bit ADC and a monitor shows 8 bits per channel. How many camera levels fall on one monitor level if the whole camera range is shown?






Answer





2^{12} / 2^8 = 4096 / 256 = 16 camera levels per monitor level. The monitor cannot show the difference between them, but the data still contain it: measure on the 12-bit numbers, not on the screenshot.




Q2. You reduce an image from 8 to 7 bits. By what factor does the RMS quantisation error grow, and what happens to the SNR in dB?






Hint





How does the step \Delta change when you remove one bit?









Answer





The step doubles (from 1/255 to 1/127 of the range, almost exactly a factor 2), so the RMS error \Delta/\sqrt{12} doubles too. The SNR drops by 20\log_{10}2 \approx 6 dB.




Q3. Why is banding easy to see in a picture of a clear blue sky, and hard to see in a picture of grass, even with the same bit depth?






Answer





In the sky, brightness changes slowly over many pixels, so many neighbouring pixels round the same way and the steps line up into visible contour lines. In the grass, the brightness changes a lot from pixel to pixel; the rounding error is different for each pixel and looks like (invisible) noise. The texture acts as a natural dither.




Q4. Adding random noise before rounding (dithering) makes the RMS error larger. Why do we do it anyway?






Answer





Without dither, the error follows the image: it forms bands that look like edges that are not there, and a value between two levels is always pushed the same way (a bias). With dither, the error is independent of the image and has mean zero for every grey value, so averaging over a region (or by the eye) recovers grey values between the levels. Structured error is worse than a slightly larger random error.

title: Segmentation as energy minimisation
text:
About this lecture
Segmentation: decide for every pixel whether it belongs to the object or to the background.

Recall thresholding (the thresholding day), and why noise breaks it.
A segmentation as a labelling L, and a number E(L) that says how good it is.
Two terms: pixels should match an intensity model, and agree with their neighbours.
One weight \lambda trades the two off.
On a 1D line the best labelling can be found exactly by dynamic programming. On an image we need more: graph cuts, the next units.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

title: Segmentation as energy minimisation
section: Recall: thresholding and its noise specks
text:
Recall: thresholding and its noise specks
Thresholding (the thresholding day): every pixel brighter than a grey level \tau is object, L_p = 1 if I_p > \tau, else L_p = 0.

Each pixel is decided on its own. With noise the two histogram peaks overlap, and pixels in the overlap land on the wrong side: isolated specks of object in the background, holes in the object.
Real objects are mostly connected: a pixel usually has the same label as its neighbours. Thresholding cannot use that; this lecture adds it.


One-slide recall: the histogram, threshold choice (Otsu, minimum error) and evaluation are taught on the thresholding day. Here only the failure matters, because it motivates the smoothness term. The demo’s “λ = 0: threshold” preset shows the specks.

title: Segmentation as energy minimisation
text:
A labelling and its energy
A segmentation is a labelling L = (L_1, \dots, L_n), L_p \in \{0, 1\}. Give each one a cost:
E(L) = \underbrace{\sum_p D_p(L_p)}_{\text{data term}} \;+\; \lambda \underbrace{\sum_{(p,q)\ \text{neighbours}} w_{pq}\,[L_p \neq L_q]}_{\text{smoothness term}}

D_p(\ell): the cost of giving pixel p the label \ell, from its intensity.
[L_p \ne L_q] is 1 if the neighbours disagree, else 0. The sum counts the boundary: with w_{pq} = 1 it is the boundary length in pixel edges.
\lambda \ge 0 sets how much a unit of boundary costs, in units of the data term.

The segmentation is the labelling with the smallest energy.

title: Segmentation as energy minimisation
section: The data term from an intensity model
text:
The data term from an intensity model
Model the intensities: background pixels are \mathcal N(\mu_0, s^2), object pixels \mathcal N(\mu_1, s^2). Take
D_p(\ell) = -\log P(I_p \mid \ell) = \frac{(I_p - \mu_\ell)^2}{2 s^2} + \text{const}.

Likely intensities are cheap, unlikely ones expensive. The constant is the same for both labels, so it does not change which labelling wins.
With \lambda = 0 every pixel takes its cheaper label: L_p = 1 exactly when (I_p - \mu_1)^2 < (I_p - \mu_0)^2, that is when I_p > \tfrac12(\mu_0 + \mu_1).
So \lambda = 0 is thresholding, at the grey level where the two Gaussians cross.

Other models (a histogram, unequal widths, colour) change only D_p, not the method.

title: Segmentation as energy minimisation
text:
The smoothness term
\lambda \sum_{(p,q)} w_{pq}\,[L_p \neq L_q]

An isolated wrong pixel has 4 disagreeing neighbours: flipping it saves 4\lambda of boundary and costs only its data difference |D_p(1) - D_p(0)|.
Small \lambda: close to thresholding; noise survives.
Large \lambda: boundaries are expensive; specks and holes vanish, but so do thin real structures, and corners get rounded.
Very large \lambda: no boundary at all, so everything gets one label.

The weights w_{pq} can depend on the image: make a boundary cheap where the image has an edge (next units).

title: Segmentation as energy minimisation
text:
A small example by hand
A 1\times5 image I = (3, 3, 1, 3, 0), \mu_0 = 0, \mu_1 = 3, D_p(\ell) = (I_p - \mu_\ell)^2:

Thresholding gives L = 11010: data 0 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 0 = 1, 3 boundaries: E = 1 + 3\lambda.
Filling the dark pixel, L = 11110: data 4, 1 boundary: E = 4 + \lambda.
The second wins when 4 + \lambda < 1 + 3\lambda, i.e. \lambda > 1.5. Above \lambda = 9, all object (E = 13) wins.

title: Segmentation as energy minimisation
section: Try it: a noisy line profile
text:
Try it: a noisy line profile




A line of 80 samples: a cell (bright) and a thin bright structure, 2 samples wide, on a dark background, with noise. Dashed lines: the two levels μ0 and μ1; dotted: the threshold halfway. The three strips are the true labels, thresholding, and the labelling with the smallest energy; black dots mark wrong samples. Tour: press “λ = 0: threshold”, 3 wrong samples and 10 boundaries. Then “λ = 3”: no wrong samples, 4 boundaries; point out that the data cost went UP (40.4 to 47.3) but the total went down. “Thin structure lost”: at λ = 10 the 2-sample structure is gone, because keeping it costs 2 boundaries. “Too smooth”: λ = 100, one boundary left. Finally move μ1 down to about 110: the threshold moves and errors return.

title: Segmentation as energy minimisation
text:
The math: the probabilistic view
Minimising E is finding the most probable labelling (a maximum a posteriori estimate):
P(L \mid I) \;\propto\; P(I \mid L)\,P(L) \;\propto\; \exp\!\big(-E(L)\big)

P(I \mid L) = \prod_p P(I_p \mid L_p), the intensity model, gives the data term.
P(L) \propto \exp\!\big(-\lambda \sum w_{pq} [L_p \ne L_q]\big), a prior that prefers few boundaries. This is a Markov random field: each label depends directly only on its neighbours.
Taking -\log turns the product into the sum E(L).

title: Segmentation as energy minimisation
section: How do we find the minimum?
text:
How do we find the minimum?
There are 2^n labellings. A 100\times100 image has 2^{10000} \approx 10^{3010}: trying them all is hopeless.
But the energy has structure: each term involves one pixel or two neighbours.

On a 1D chain (a line of pixels), that structure is enough for dynamic programming: walk along the line once, keeping for each pixel only the best energy so far for “this pixel object” and “this pixel background”. Exact, and fast.
On a 2D grid the neighbours form loops, and dynamic programming no longer works.
For two labels, E can still be minimised exactly: as a minimum cut in a graph. That is the next two units.

title: Segmentation as energy minimisation
section: The math: dynamic programming on a chain
text:
The math: dynamic programming on a chain
On a chain, E(L) = \sum_k D_k(L_k) + \lambda \sum_k [L_k \ne L_{k+1}]. Let C_k(\ell) be the smallest energy of pixels 1..k with L_k = \ell:
C_1(\ell) = D_1(\ell), \qquad C_k(\ell) = D_k(\ell) + \min\big(C_{k-1}(\ell),\; C_{k-1}(1 - \ell) + \lambda\big).

Fill a 2 \times n table from left to right, remembering which choice won.
The minimum energy is \min_\ell C_n(\ell); follow the remembered choices back to read off L.
Example above, \lambda = 2: C(0) = 9, 11, 3, 12, 6 and C(1) = 0, 0, 4, 4, 13. Minimum 6, labelling 11110.

This is the Viterbi algorithm; the demo uses exactly this.

title: Segmentation as energy minimisation
text:
Summary

Thresholding decides each pixel alone; noise gives specks and holes.
Segmentation as energy minimisation: E(L) = \sum_p D_p(L_p) + \lambda \sum w_{pq}[L_p \ne L_q].
Data term = -\log P(I_p \mid \ell); for two Gaussians, \lambda = 0 is thresholding at the crossing point.
\lambda trades fidelity for boundary length: too large removes thin structures, then everything.
Exact minimisation: dynamic programming on a chain; on a grid, graph cuts, next.

title: Exercise: generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

generate images by decoding draws from the prior, and say which draws are likely,
interpolate between two images in latent space and explain why the latent midpoint is not the pixel average,
read a 2D latent space: neighbours, overlaps, and what the axes do (not) mean,
use the reconstruction error for anomaly detection, and decoding for denoising, and name their limits.

The questions under By hand and Explore are for everyone. The Math questions (derive, prove) are for students who want the full treatment.

title: Exercise: generating and exploring images with a VAE

By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

read a 2D latent space: neighbours, overlaps, and what the axes do (not) mean,

The questions under By hand and Explore are for everyone. The Math questions (derive, prove) are for students who want the full treatment.

title: Exercise: generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
Background







Word
Meaning




Generate
draw z \sim \mathcal N(0, I), decode


Latent walk
decode z(t) = (1 - t)\,z_A + t\,z_B for t from 0 to 1


Pixel fade
(1 - t)\,x_A + t\,x_B, the images themselves averaged


Reconstruction error
mean squared pixel error between an image and the decoded centre of its cloud


Anomaly score
the reconstruction error; above a threshold set on normal images → “unusual”


Denoising
encode a noisy image, decode the centre of its cloud



The two models of the demo: a 2D VAE trained on MNIST handwritten digits, and a 2D VAE trained on synthetic cell masks (round, elongated, dividing, with a protrusion). Both: 28\times28 images, encoder 784 \to 192 \to 2, decoder 2 \to 192 \to 784.

title: Exercise: generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
By hand

Part A — walks and midpoints
A decoder draws a bright bar on a 3-pixel image: pixel i (i = 0, 1, 2) gets \max(0,\ 1 - |z - i|).
B1. Let z_A = 0 and z_B = 2. Write z(t) for t = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, and decode each.
B2. Compute the pixel fade at t = 0.5. Compare with the decoded latent midpoint. Which one is an image of “a bar”?
B3. A linear decoder (PCA) maps z(t) to the pixel fade exactly. Explain why, using \text{decode}(z) = \bar{\mathbf x} + z\,\mathbf u.


Part B — generating
B4. New images are made by drawing z from the 2D prior \mathcal N(0, I). The probability that a draw lands within radius r of 0 is 1 - e^{-r^2/2}. What fraction of draws lands within radius 1, 2 and 3?
B5. The demo’s “far outside” point is z = (3.3,\ -3.3). How much less probable is a draw near this point than a draw near 0 (ratio of the prior densities)? What does the decoder output there, and should we trust it?


Part C — applications
B6. On 2000 normal test masks of the cell-shape VAE, 95% have reconstruction error below 0.0295 and 99% below 0.0447. You set the threshold at 0.0447. About how many of 2000 normal cells are flagged (false alarms)? Which of these is flagged: a ring (error 0.172), two separate cells in one crop (0.253), a square cell (0.030)?
B7. Explain why the square is not flagged, although no training cell was square. What kind of anomaly can a reconstruction-error detector not see?
B8. Explain in two sentences why decoding a noisy image removes the noise, and what it may remove besides the noise.






Solutions





B1. z(t) = 2t: z = 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, decoded (1, 0, 0), (0.5, 0.5, 0), (0, 1, 0), (0, 0.5, 0.5), (0, 0, 1). The bar moves from left to right (smeared over two pixels when it is between them).
B2. Pixel fade at t = 0.5: \tfrac12(1, 0, 0) + \tfrac12(0, 0, 1) = (0.5,\ 0,\ 0.5): two half-bright bars, a double exposure. The latent midpoint decodes to (0, 1, 0): one bar in the middle. Only the latent midpoint is an image of a bar.
B3. \text{decode}\big((1-t)z_A + tz_B\big) = \bar{\mathbf x} + \big((1-t)z_A + tz_B\big)\mathbf u = (1-t)(\bar{\mathbf x} + z_A\mathbf u) + t(\bar{\mathbf x} + z_B\mathbf u), which is the pixel fade of the two decoded images. A linear map preserves straight lines and averages; only a curved decoder can turn a straight latent line into a moving bar.
B4. Radius 1: 1 - e^{-0.5} = 0.393. Radius 2: 1 - e^{-2} = 0.865. Radius 3: 1 - e^{-4.5} = 0.989. About 1 draw in 90 lands outside radius 3.
B5. The density ratio is e^{-(3.3^2 + 3.3^2)/2} = e^{-10.89} \approx 0.00002: about 50,000 times less probable per unit area than near 0. The decoder still outputs an image (for the digits a thin slanted stroke), because it always answers; but almost no training images were encoded there, so nothing says the image is a realistic digit.
B6. 1% of 2000, about 20 false alarms. The ring (0.172) and the two cells (0.253) are flagged; the square (0.030) is not.
B7. A square is close enough to a large round cell that the decoder rebuilds it as one with only a small error (mostly at the corners). The detector only sees anomalies that the decoder cannot draw; an unusual image that happens to look like a normal one in the squared-error sense passes. Anomalies in a small detail (a tiny dark spot) are also hard to see, because they change few pixels.
B8. The decoder can only draw images like those it was trained on, and pixel noise is not among them, so the decoded image is a clean cell. But it is the model’s version of the cell: details it never learned or cannot store in two numbers (a thin protrusion, an exact outline) are replaced by typical ones, and if the noise moves the code to the wrong region, the output is the wrong shape.





Math questions
B9. (math) Several different images x share (almost) the same code z. Show that the single output c minimising \mathbb E\big[\|x - c\|^2\big] is c = \mathbb E[x], and use this to explain why VAE images are blurry.






Solutions (math)





B9. (math) \mathbb E\|x - c\|^2 = \mathbb E\|(x - \mathbb E x) + (\mathbb E x - c)\|^2 = \mathbb E\|x - \mathbb E x\|^2 + \|\mathbb E x - c\|^2 (the cross term has mean zero). Only the second term depends on c, and it is zero at c = \mathbb E x. So the decoder’s best output for a z shared by several images is their average, and the average of differently placed sharp strokes or outlines is a blurred one. Wider clouds (larger \beta) make more images share each z: more blur.

title: Exercise: generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
Explore
The demo has two tabs with fixed, pre-trained weights. Left: the latent space with the cloud centres of 1000 test images coloured by class (labels at the class centres) and the prior’s radius-2 circle (dashed). Drag z or click in the map: the large image is decoded from z. Draw an image in the dashed box (or press example ▸) and the encoder places it: the cross is the cloud centre, the orange ellipse its ±2 sd; the error under the encoder input is its reconstruction error. The strip below shows a walk z → z′, draws from the encoder’s cloud, or draws from the prior. noise on input adds noise (fixed seed) to the encoder input.



Data: MNIST handwritten digits (Y. LeCun, C. Cortes, C. J. C. Burges; CC BY-SA 3.0 as stated in the Keras documentation); the 20 example digits are MNIST test images. The cell masks are synthetic, generated by the training script.
E1. Digits. Press example ▸ a few times. Where do the 0s and 1s land, and how big are the clouds? Then draw your own 4 and encode it. Is its reconstruction a 4?
E2. Preset walk 1 → 7, then walk 0 → 1. Describe the strips. Which digits does the 0 → 1 walk pass through, and why?
E3. Press sample from the prior a few times. Are all generated images digits? Then tick decoded grid: where in the map do the images stop looking like digits?
E4. Switch to Cell shapes. Tick decoded grid and describe how the shapes change across the map. Press walk round → dividing.
E5. Cell shapes: step example ▸ through all 15 examples and note the errors. Which kind of normal cell has the largest errors, and what does the reconstruction lose? Which of the three anomalies (examples 13–15) would a threshold of 0.045 flag?
E6. Cell shapes: load example 2 (a round cell), then set noise on input to 0.3. Compare the encoder input, the decoded image and the error. Repeat with example 4 (an elongated cell). Then try the same in the digits tab.






Solutions





E1. The first two examples are 0s, landing at the lower left (centres (-2.48, -1.56) and (-2.19, -2.03)); the 1s land on the right ((2.15, 0.37), (2.00, -0.78)). The clouds are tiny: spreads 0.07–0.13 per axis for these four (the mean over all test digits is 0.067): one image says a lot about its z. Your own 4 depends on your drawing: 4s land in the crowded region around (0.6, 0.35), next to the 9s, and often come back looking like a 9.
E2. 1 → 7: a 1, then a 1 that grows a hook, a 9-like shape, and a 7: every step is digit-like. 0 → 1 passes 0, 6, 2, 5, 9, a faint smudge and 1: the straight line from the 0s (lower left) to the 1s (right) crosses the regions of 6, 2, 5 and 9 on its way. The second-to-last step is faint because it lies in the sparse region below the crowded middle, where few digits are encoded.
E3. Most samples are digits (the first press gives 2, 6, 9, 9, an unclear 7/5-like stroke, 1, 5), but some are blends or blurred, from points between classes. In the grid, the bottom middle (around z_2 < -2, |z_1| < 1) decodes to smudges: almost no test digits are encoded there (1 of the 1000 shown).
E4. Large round cells on the left, smaller and more elongated cells to the right, with the orientation of the long axis changing around the map; dividing cells (dumbbells) along the bottom. Protrusions do not appear as a separate region. The walk round → dividing goes through slightly elongated cells to a waisted dumbbell: a smooth change of shape.
E5. Normal cells: 0.004–0.023. The cells with a protrusion have the largest errors (0.023, 0.016, 0.021): the reconstruction is a round or oval cell without the thin protrusion. Anomalies: ring 0.172 and two cells 0.253 are flagged (their codes, (-6.30, 3.49) and (-4.18, -0.36), lie outside the map; the cross is not visible); the square (0.030) is not.
E6. Example 2 with noise 0.3: the encoder input is speckled, the decoded image is a clean round cell, and the error (against the clean mask) is 0.009, against 0.045 for the noisy input itself. Example 4: the noisy code lands elsewhere and the decoded cell has the wrong orientation: error 0.110, worse than the noisy input (0.047). In the digits tab the decoded image is also free of speckle, but often a different or blurrier digit; in squared error it is usually worse than the noisy input, because the digit reconstructions are blurry even without noise (mean error 0.041 over the test set).

title: Exercise: generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
Where this leads

Bigger latent spaces (10–100 dimensions) rebuild far more detail; the 2D maps here are for looking, not for best quality.
Conditional VAEs also give the decoder a label (a digit class, a treatment), so it can generate “a 7” or “a treated cell” on demand.
GANs and diffusion models generate much sharper images; diffusion models learn to remove noise step by step and are behind most current image generators.
Morphology spaces: autoencoder latent spaces of cell and nucleus images are used to compare treatments and find unusual cells in large screens.

title: Quiz: generating and exploring images with a VAE
text:
Short questions on generating, interpolating and using a trained VAE. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. How do you generate a new image with a trained VAE?






Hint





Which part of the network do you need, and where does its input come from?









Answer





Draw z from the prior \mathcal N(0, I) and pass it through the decoder. The encoder is not needed.




Q2. True or false: the latent midpoint of two images always decodes to the pixel average of the two images.






Hint





True for a linear decoder. Is the VAE decoder linear?









Answer





False. A linear decoder (PCA) maps the midpoint to the average, a double exposure. A curved decoder maps it to an in-between shape: a bar halfway, a digit halfway between a 1 and a 7.




Q3. A colleague names the latent axes of a 2D VAE “z_1 = thickness” and “z_2 = slant”. What is the problem?






Hint





Does the loss change if the latent space is rotated?









Answer





The prior \mathcal N(0, I) and the KL penalty look the same after a rotation of the latent space, so the axes have no fixed meaning; another training run could give rotated or flipped axes. Directions should be read from decoded images along them, and need not line up with the axes.




Q4. Why are the images from a VAE blurrier than the training images?






Hint





What single image best matches several different images in squared error?









Answer





Several training images share each region of latent space, and the decoder outputs one image for it. The output that minimises the average squared error is their average, and an average of slightly different sharp images is blurred.




Q5. You use reconstruction error to find unusual cells. Name one kind of unusual cell this will catch and one it may miss.






Hint





What can the decoder draw?









Answer





It catches shapes the decoder cannot draw (a ring, two cells in one crop: large error). It misses unusual cells that happen to look like a normal one in squared error (a square close to a round cell), and small details that change few pixels.




Q6. What does increasing \beta do to generated images and to the latent space?






Hint





Stronger pull towards the prior.









Answer





The latent space gets smoother and better filled, with directions that often follow one factor each; the images get blurrier and more average.

title: The variational autoencoder
text:
About this lecture
An autoencoder gives every image a point z. A variational autoencoder (VAE) gives every image a small cloud, and keeps all clouds near one standard bell shape.

Why: so that every point of the latent space decodes to a plausible image, and we can generate new ones.
How: the decoder is trained on random draws from each cloud (the reparameterisation trick).
The loss has two parts: rebuild the image + stay close to the standard cloud (a KL divergence).

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Concept layer first on every topic, then a “The math” slide that can be skipped. Weaker students should leave with: cloud instead of point, decoder sees random draws, two forces (rebuild vs stay near the prior), and what β does. Reference: D. P. Kingma, M. Welling (2014), Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes, ICLR, arXiv:1312.6114; Rezende, Mohamed & Wierstra (2014) independently.

title: The variational autoencoder
text:
What a plain autoencoder lacks
A plain autoencoder only has to rebuild its training images. It may place them anywhere in z.

Nothing says what lies between two training images: decode a point in a gap and the result can be anything, often a smudge that is no digit at all.
Nothing says where the images are: to generate a new image, which z should we pick?
Each image is one point, with no notion of how sure the encoder is.

We want: similar images nearby, no gaps, and a known region to draw new z from.

Draw on the board: a 2D latent space with a few dots for 1s and 7s scattered with gaps between; pick a point in a gap; the decoder was never trained there. Then draw what we want: the same dots packed into one round region, 1s and 7s side by side, so the point between a 1 and a 7 decodes to something in between.

title: The variational autoencoder
section: A cloud instead of a point
text:
A cloud instead of a point
The encoder outputs, for each image x, a centre \mu(x) and a spread \sigma(x): a Gaussian cloud q(z \mid x) = \mathcal N\big(\mu(x),\ \sigma(x)^2\big).

During training the decoder is handed a random point of the cloud, not the centre, and must still rebuild this image.
So every point near an image must decode to something like it: the space around each image gets trained.
A penalty pulls every cloud towards one standard cloud \mathcal N(0, I), the prior. Clouds overlap, gaps fill.

Two forces: rebuild well (small, separate clouds) against look like the prior (wide, overlapping clouds near 0).

This is the whole idea. The rebuild force alone would shrink each cloud to a point and push them apart: a plain autoencoder. The prior force alone would make every cloud the standard cloud, and the decoder could not tell images apart: every image decoded as the average image. The balance gives a latent space where every region is used and neighbouring points decode to similar images.

title: The variational autoencoder
text:
The result on handwritten digits




A VAE with a 2D latent space trained on 60,000 handwritten digits (MNIST). Dots: the cloud centres of 1000 test digits; orange: the clouds (±2 sd) of six test digits.

Digits of one kind sit together; similar digits (4, 9; 3, 5, 8) are neighbours.
Almost everything lies inside the prior’s dashed circle: no big gaps.
The clouds are small (sd about 0.07): the image says a lot about z.



Real network (784 → 192 → 2, decoder 2 → 192 → 784), trained offline with a fixed seed; the same weights run in the demos. The mean encoder sd over the 10,000 test digits is 0.067. 71.5% of the test centres lie inside radius 2; a standard 2D normal has 86.5% there (1 − e^{−2}). MNIST: Y. LeCun, C. Cortes, C. J. C. Burges; CC BY-SA 3.0 as stated in the Keras documentation.

title: The variational autoencoder
text:
The reparameterisation trick
How do we draw “a random point of the cloud” and still train by walking downhill?
z = \mu + \sigma\,\varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal N(0, 1).

Draw the randomness \varepsilon first, from a fixed bell curve; then shift and stretch it.
Example: \mu = 1, \sigma = 0.5: \varepsilon = -1 gives z = 0.5; \varepsilon = 0.5 gives z = 1.25.
z is now an ordinary formula in \mu and \sigma, so the gradient flows back through it to the encoder.


If we drew z directly from N(mu, sigma²), the draw would be a black box: how does the result change if mu changes a little? Writing z = mu + sigma·eps answers it: dz/dmu = 1, dz/dsigma = eps. In the demo elbo1d the 20 orange dots are z = mu + s·eps with 20 fixed eps; dragging mu shifts them all, dragging s stretches them around mu.

title: The variational autoencoder
section: How far is a cloud from the prior?
text:
How far is a cloud from the prior?
The penalty is the Kullback–Leibler divergence \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p): zero when the two distributions are equal, positive otherwise. For a 1D cloud \mathcal N(\mu, s^2) and the prior \mathcal N(0, 1):
\mathrm{KL} = \tfrac12\big(\mu^2 + s^2 - 1 - \ln s^2\big)

Moving the centre away from 0 costs \tfrac12\mu^2; a cloud much narrower (or wider) than 1 costs too.

The three cases: the prior itself (KL 0); the best cloud of the demo’s default example (mu 1.2, s 0.45: KL 1.12); a narrow cloud away from 0 (mu −1.5, s 0.15: KL 2.53). In 2D (or k dimensions) with independent coordinates, the KLs add. The formula is on this slide so the exercises can use it; the derivation is on the next slide.

title: The variational autoencoder
section: The math: KL of two Gaussians
text:
The math: KL of two Gaussians
\mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p) = \mathbb E_{q}\big[\ln q(z) - \ln p(z)\big]. With q = \mathcal N(\mu, s^2) and p = \mathcal N(0, 1):
\ln q(z) = -\tfrac12\ln(2\pi s^2) - \frac{(z-\mu)^2}{2s^2}, \qquad \ln p(z) = -\tfrac12\ln(2\pi) - \frac{z^2}{2}.
Use \mathbb E_q[(z-\mu)^2] = s^2 and \mathbb E_q[z^2] = \mu^2 + s^2:
\mathrm{KL} = -\tfrac12\ln s^2 - \tfrac12 + \tfrac12(\mu^2 + s^2) = \tfrac12\big(\mu^2 + s^2 - 1 - \ln s^2\big).

\ge 0, with equality only at \mu = 0, s = 1 (since s^2 - 1 - \ln s^2 \ge 0).
Not symmetric: \mathrm{KL}(q\|p) \ne \mathrm{KL}(p\|q) in general.

title: The variational autoencoder
text:
The VAE loss
For every training image x, with z = \mu(x) + \sigma(x)\,\varepsilon:
\text{loss}(x) = \underbrace{\text{reconstruction error of } \text{decode}(z)}_{\text{rebuild this image}} \;+\; \beta\cdot\underbrace{\mathrm{KL}\big(q(z\mid x)\,\|\,\mathcal N(0, I)\big)}_{\text{stay near the prior}}

Reconstruction: squared pixel error (Gaussian pixel noise), or the cross-entropy when the decoder outputs an “ink probability” per pixel, as for digits.
\beta = 1 is the standard VAE. Larger \beta: tidier latent space, blurrier images. Smaller \beta: sharper, but gaps return.
Encoder and decoder are trained together, downhill on the average loss.


Concept slide: the two forces of slide 3 written as one number to minimise. The next slide (math layer) shows where it comes from: with beta = 1 and the right reconstruction term, the loss is minus a lower bound on log p(x), the evidence lower bound (ELBO).

title: The variational autoencoder
section: The math: where the loss comes from (ELBO)
text:
The math: where the loss comes from (ELBO)
Model: z \sim p(z) = \mathcal N(0, I), image x \sim p(x\mid z) (the decoder). We would like to maximise \ln p(x) = \ln\int p(x\mid z)\,p(z)\,dz, but the integral is intractable. For any q(z):
\ln p(x) = \ln \mathbb E_{q}\!\left[\frac{p(x\mid z)\,p(z)}{q(z)}\right] \;\ge\; \mathbb E_{q}\big[\ln p(x\mid z)\big] - \mathrm{KL}\big(q\,\|\,p\big) \;=:\; \text{ELBO}
by Jensen’s inequality (\ln is concave). The gap is exactly \mathrm{KL}\big(q(z)\,\|\,p(z\mid x)\big) \ge 0.

Maximising the ELBO over the decoder makes the images likely; over q it makes q approach the posterior p(z\mid x). The VAE loss is -\text{ELBO} (with \beta = 1).
Gaussian decoder p(x\mid z) = \mathcal N(\text{decode}(z), \sigma_x^2 I): -\ln p(x\mid z) = \frac{\|x - \text{decode}(z)\|^2}{2\sigma_x^2} + \text{const}, the squared error.
“Variational”: q is chosen from a family (Gaussians) to make the bound tight; the encoder outputs it in one pass for every x (“amortised”).


Proof of the gap: ln p(x) − ELBO = E_q[ln q(z) − ln p(z|x)] using p(x|z)p(z) = p(z|x)p(x). So the bound is tight exactly when q is the true posterior. Bayesian reading in one sentence for the concept layer: the standard cloud is the prior, each image’s cloud an approximate posterior.

A VAE you can solve by hand
One grey value x and a 1D latent z. Decoder: \hat x = w z with w = 1 and pixel noise \sigma_x = 0.5. Observed x = 1.5.

Ignoring the image costs reconstruction; being too sure costs KL. The best cloud sits between the prior and the image.

Rebuild term = ((x − w mu)² + w² s²)/(2 sx²): the expected squared error over the cloud, divided by 2 sx². At the prior: (2.25 + 1)/0.5 = 6.5. Too confident: (0 + 0.0025)/0.5 = 0.005, but KL = ½(2.25 + 0.0025 − 1 − ln 0.0025) = 3.622. Best: mu = 1.2, s² = 0.2. The best cloud is the exact posterior of z given x for this model (math slide after the demo).

title: The variational autoencoder
text:
Try it: the two forces




Start: q = prior, total 6.5. Drag mu towards x: reconstruction falls fast, KL rises slowly. Shrink s: the decoded blue dots gather around x, the reconstruction falls, KL rises. “best cloud” jumps to mu 1.2, s 0.447, total 1.705. Preset “best (β = 5)”: mu 0.667, s 0.745: the cloud is pulled towards the prior; the reconstruction term rises to 2.5. The readout also shows the reconstruction estimated from the 20 draws (what training actually uses): at the prior it is 8.52 instead of 6.5, a noisy estimate of the same number.

title: The variational autoencoder
text:
The math: the best cloud
L(\mu, s) = \frac{(x - w\mu)^2 + w^2 s^2}{2\sigma_x^2} + \frac{\beta}{2}\big(\mu^2 + s^2 - 1 - \ln s^2\big)

\partial L/\partial\mu = 0: \ \mu^* = \dfrac{w\,x}{w^2 + \beta\sigma_x^2}. \qquad\partial L/\partial (s^2) = 0: \ s^{*2} = \dfrac{\beta\sigma_x^2}{\beta\sigma_x^2 + w^2}.
Numbers (w = 1, \sigma_x = 0.5, x = 1.5): \beta = 1: \mu^* = 1.2, s^{*2} = 0.2. \beta = 5: \mu^* = 0.667, s^{*2} = 0.556.
For \beta = 1 this is exactly the Bayesian posterior of z given x (a product of two Gaussians): here the bound is tight. Larger \beta pulls q towards the prior.

title: The variational autoencoder
text:
Summary







Idea
In one line




Cloud
the encoder gives each image a centre \mu and a spread \sigma


Reparameterisation
z = \mu + \sigma\varepsilon: randomness first, so gradients flow


Prior
one standard cloud \mathcal N(0, I) that all clouds are pulled towards


KL
\tfrac12(\mu^2 + s^2 - 1 - \ln s^2) per dimension; 0 only for the prior


Loss
reconstruction +\ \beta\cdotKL; \beta = 1 is the standard VAE


Two forces
rebuild well (small, separate clouds) vs. look like the prior (wide, overlapping)



Next: use the trained decoder to generate, interpolate and detect unusual images.
